title: The First Deep Learning all-sky List of Fermi-LAT Gamma-ray Sources
authors: Saptashwa Bhattacharyya, Giacomo Principe, Dmitry Malyshev, Roberto Ruiz de Austri, Gabrijela Zaharijas, Sascha Caron, Fiorenzo Stoppa, Guðlaugur Johannesson
abstract: Aims: We develop a deep-learning-based pipeline to construct a list of {\gamma}-ray sources and to quantitatively assess the impact of background uncertainties on source detection and characterization. This work extends and enhances the existing AutoSource-ID algorithm, previously adopted on optical observations, for applications on {\gamma}-ray data. Methods: Source detection was performed through image segmentation using a U-Net architecture, while dedicated deep neural networks (DNNs) were employed for source localization, flux estimation, and the classification of detected sources as either genuine or spurious. The training data were generated from Monte Carlo simulations based on 10 years of Fermi-LAT observations. Results: We present the first Fermi-LAT {\gamma}-ray all-sky source list derived using a deep-learning-based method (1FDL), containing more than 3800 sources with estimated positions, fluxes, and probability scores that quantify the likelihood of each detection being genuine or spurious. We further evaluated the robustness of the pipeline against variations in the interstellar emission model (IEM) and compared the resulting source list with the 4FGL-DR2 catalog. Conclusion: We find that the our deep-learning-based approach achieves performance comparable to, or better than, the likelihood-based methods employed in the standard Fermi-LAT catalog pipeline when tested against changes in the IEM. The 1FDL source list is broadly consistent with the Fermi-LAT 4FGL-DR2 catalog obtained over the same 10-year observational period, including a few new sources confirmed in the recent Fermi-LAT 16-year source list (FL16Y). These results demonstrate the potential of DNN methods for the detection and characterization of {\gamma}-ray sources and provide a foundation for their application in future high-energy astrophysical analyses.

title: $γ$-ray variability of changing-look blazars: FSRQ-like jet behaviour
authors: Zahoor Malik, B. van Soelen, Sikandar Akbar, Zahir Shah
abstract: Changing-look blazars (CLBs) move between the flat-spectrum radio quasar (FSRQ) and BL Lacertae (BL Lac) optical classifications. Either the accretion flow switches regime, or a brightening jet continuum swamps the broad lines while the system itself is unchanged. The two pictures predict the same optical behaviour but differ in the jet, so the $\gamma$-ray emission could potentially separate them. Catalogue quantities averaged over the mission cannot, because a permanently intermediate source and one alternating between two states return the same mean. We therefore use 17.9\,yr of \textit{Fermi}-LAT light curves at 3-, 7- and 30-day cadence, comparing CLBs with BL Lac and FSRQ controls selected and analysed identically. CLBs and FSRQs have indistinguishable fractional variability, with medians of 0.483 and 0.437 at 30-day cadence ($p = 0.94$), while BL Lacs are far less variable at 0.262 ($p = 1.4\times10^{-4}$). The result survives restricting the controls to low-synchrotron-peaked sources and matching in flux and sampling. Several further diagnostics group CLBs with FSRQs, as does their Eddington-scaled disc luminosity. Followed through time, CLB light curves show no excess of bimodal flux distributions, and the direction of the optical transition does not predict how the $\gamma$-ray spectrum evolves. CLBs do reach hard, BL Lac-like spectra more often than FSRQs, but never for longer than chance allows. Only in this, and in how their spectra respond to brightening, do they fall between the two classes. The changing-look phenomenon therefore leaves little imprint on the $\gamma$-ray jet, favouring a variable jet continuum over a change of accretion regime.
comments: 18 pages, 15 figures, Submitted

figs.cap: Cumulative distributions of the fractional variability amplitude $F_{\rm var}$ for the three samples, at 3-day (left), 7-day (middle) and 30-day (right) cadence. Blue denotes BL Lacs, orange FSRQs and green CLBs. The number of sources contributing to each curve is given in Section 2.3. The shaded band around each curve is the 68 per cent confidence region obtained by bootstrap resampling of the sources, and indicates how much the curve would move under a different draw from the same population. The short vertical tick on each curve marks the median. The KS probabilities for the CLB–FSRQ and CLB–BL Lac comparisons at each cadence are listed in Table 1. At every cadence the CLB and FSRQ curves lie close together, while the BL Lac curve is displaced towards lower variability, that is, it rises earlier. Note that both axes are the same in all three panels; in particular the horizontal ($F_{\rm var}$) axis spans 0–1.3 throughout, so the leftward shift of all three curves at shorter cadence reflects the smaller variability amplitude measured on shorter timescales.

Distribution of $F_{\rm var}$ at 30-day cadence, shown as kernel density estimates offset vertically for clarity. Each curve is normalised to the same peak height, so the vertical extent carries no information and only the horizontal position and width should be compared. From top to bottom: the full BL Lac control, the BL Lac control restricted to low-synchrotron-peaked sources, the FSRQ control and the CLB sample. The dashed vertical line within each curve marks the median. Restricting the BL Lac control to LSP sources shifts its median slightly lower rather than towards the CLB value, which shows that the CLB–BL Lac difference is not produced by the different synchrotron peak distributions of the two samples.

Median fractional variability as a function of bin size, on a logarithmic horizontal scale. Error bars give the 68 per cent confidence interval on the median obtained by bootstrap resampling. Triangles denote CLBs, circles the two control samples. All three samples show larger amplitudes at longer binning, as expected when the light curves are dominated by red noise, and the CLB and FSRQ points track one another across the full range while the BL Lac points remain systematically lower.

Mean photon index against mean flux at 30-day cadence, for sources with at least 20 bins carrying a well-measured photon index. This is a slightly stricter requirement than the one used elsewhere in the paper, which counts bins with a usable flux. Blue circles denote BL Lacs, orange circles FSRQs and green triangles CLBs. Histograms above and to the right show the marginal distributions of flux and of photon index for each sample, normalised to unit area. The upper shaded band marks $\Gamma>2.2$ and the lower band $\Gamma<2.0$, the values adopted by Ren et al. (2024b) to identify FSRQ-like and BL Lac-like states; the unshaded strip between them is the transition region. The two control samples separate in photon index, with partial overlap in the transition strip, and overlap substantially in flux.

Photon index as a function of time for the 23 tier A CLBs with at least 25 time bins satisfying $TS\geq 25$, with one row per source and one coloured cell per 30-day time bin. This threshold is stricter than that used elsewhere in the paper, and is imposed so that each row contains enough well-measured cells to be read; the remaining tier A sources are too sparsely sampled to display in this form. Colour encodes the measured photon index on the diverging scale shown at the bottom, which is centred on $\Gamma=2.1$, the middle of the transition region; blue corresponds to hard, BL Lac-like spectra and red to soft, FSRQ-like spectra. Vertical black lines on the colour bar mark $\Gamma=2.0$ and $\Gamma=2.2$. Gaps indicate bins that fail the quality cuts. CLB source names are shown in bold; above and below the horizontal separators are the best-sampled BL Lac and FSRQ control sources, labelled and coloured by sample, included so that CLB behaviour can be judged against sources of known and stable spectral type. Rows are ordered by mean photon index within each group, so that the progression from hard to soft spectra can be followed down the panel. The control rows provide a visual reference: a source of stable spectral type appears as a row of nearly uniform colour, so departures from uniformity in the CLB rows can be judged against sources of known classification rather than in isolation. Control sources can depart from the colour typical of their class: 4FGL J1229.0$+$0202 (3C 273) is uniformly soft, while 4FGL J0957.6$+$5523 (4C $+$55.17) appears predominantly hard and has had its FSRQ classification questioned (McConville et al., 2011).

Eddington-scaled disc luminosity against fractional variability at 30-day cadence. Blue circles denote BL Lacs, orange circles FSRQs and green triangles CLBs. The horizontal axis is derived from optical spectroscopy (Paliya et al., 2021) and the vertical axis from the Fermi light curves, so the two quantities are measured independently of one another. Curves above and to the right are kernel density estimates of the marginal distributions, with dashed vertical lines marking the medians in $\log L_{\rm disk}/L_{\rm Edd}$. The dotted vertical line at $-2$ marks the approximate boundary below which accretion is expected to become radiatively inefficient. BL Lac values are $3\sigma$ upper limits, since their broad lines are undetected, so those points should be read as lying at or below the plotted position.

title: Simulations agree: the Milky Way's satellites are disrupting
authors: Alexander H. Riley, Nora Shipp, J. Sebastian Monzon, Arpit Arora, Adriana Dropulic, Gray Thoron, Oscar Agertz, Santi Roca-Fàbrega
abstract: Recent analyses of simulated Milky Way-mass galaxies have highlighted the prevalence of satellites undergoing tidal disruption. However, these have focused on single hydrodynamical codes with a number of limitations, making it unclear how generic this result is. We compare satellite disruption in four models: two cosmological hydrodynamical simulations (Auriga and FIRE), cosmological $N$-body simulations with stellar particle tagging (Aquarius), and a semi-analytic model with varying host disk properties (SatGen). For all systems, we compute the fraction of stellar mass retained by the progenitor ($f_\text{bound}$) at the present day. We find a remarkable agreement between FIRE, Aquarius, and SatGen; all predict that $\sim$20 to 30 per cent of classical-mass satellites have $f_\text{bound} < 0.9$ ($\sim$5 to 10 per cent have $f_\text{bound} < 0.5$). Satellites in Auriga experience substantially more mass loss than other simulations, which we attribute to their massive central galaxies and large satellite sizes prior to infall. In the ultra-faint regime captured by Aquarius and SatGen, disruption rates are comparable to or exceeding those for classical satellites. The ubiquity of mass loss across models presents both an exciting opportunity (a plethora of stellar streams awaiting discovery) and a nuisance (for theorists using satellite counts to constrain dark matter).
comments: 6+3 pages, 3+1 figures. Submitted to MNRAS Letters, comments are welcome

figs.cap: The stellar mass functions of satellite galaxies across all simulations considered in this work. Shaded contours correspond to the 1$\sigma$ scatter across haloes, while the solid lines are the medians. For visual clarity, we only show the SatGen scatter for the $M_{\text{d}}/M_{\text{vir}}=0.1$ model, which is similar across disc scenarios. The models span a variety of galaxy-halo connections and host properties, resulting in different stellar mass functions for satellites.

The cumulative distribution of $f_{\text{bound}}$ for classical-mass satellites across different simulation setups. Simulations with satellite systems that are the least disrupted overall will be towards the lower-right corner. We only include systems that have a total stellar mass $M_{\star}>5\times 10^{5}$ M$_{⊙}$ and a bound stellar mass of $M_{\star}^{\text{bound}}>10^{5}$ M$_{⊙}$. Shaded contours correspond to the 1$\sigma$ scatter across haloes, while the solid lines are the result considering all systems ‘stacked’. All of the models predict substantial stellar mass loss, with three (FIRE, Aquarius, and SatGen) further agreeing on the amount (within host-to-host scatter).

The cumulative distribution of $f_{\text{bound}}$ for ultra-faint satellites, shown in a similar manner as Figure 2. We only include systems that have a bound stellar mass of $10^{2}\mathrm{\,M_{\odot}}<M_{\star}^{\text{bound}}<10^{5}\mathrm{\,M_{\odot}}$. The result for FIRE classical-mass satellites is also shown for comparison. Ultra-faint satellites experience stellar mass loss comparable to, or exceeding, those for classicals.

The cumulative distribution of $f_{\text{bound}}$ for satellites across different simulation setups. The information is the same as is presented in Figures 2 and 3, but each panel corresponds to a different simulation. Simulations that produce particle distributions (Auriga, FIRE, Aquarius) have each individual haloes shown as a thin lines. The SatGen realizations are shown as shaded contours, corresponding to the 1$\sigma$ percentiles across all 500 haloes. The medians across all haloes are shown as thick dashed lines, while the stacked distributions (what is shown in the main text) are shown as thick solid lines. Despite substantial differences the galaxy-halo connections and other modeling choices, all of the simulations predict substantial stellar mass loss for satellites of Milky Way-mass haloes.

title: A Large Diversity in the Quiescent Fractions of Massive Galaxies in Proto-clusters at $z\sim4-6$ in the FRESCO GOODS fields
authors: Jamie Lin, Danilo Marchesini, Pascal A. Oesch, Rohan P. Naidu, Alba Covelo-Paz, Gabriel Brammer, Thomas Herard-Demanche, Christian Kragh Jespersen, Andrea Weibel, Kate Whitaker, Mengyuan Xiao
abstract: To constrain the emergence of the first quiescent galaxies (QGs) and their connection to large-scale structure, we search for rare, high-redshift QGs in proto-clusters using spectral energy distribution modeling, multiple rest-frame color diagnostics, and visual inspection. Our sample includes 12 QG candidates with stellar masses log(M*/Msun) ~ 9-11 in four proto-clusters at z ~ 4-6 within GOODS-North (GOODS-N) and GOODS-South (GOODS-S). The selection uses 11 NIRCam filters in GOODS-N and 17 NIRCam plus 2 MIRI filters in GOODS-S, combined with 9 ancillary HST filters, covering 0.4-7.7 microns. We measure an increasing quiescent fraction with stellar mass, with averages of 1.0%(+0.7/-0.4; 5/502), 3.5%(+2.8/-1.7; 4/115), and 33.3%(+22.2/-17.5; 3/9) for log(M*/Msun) = 9 - 9.75, 9.75 - 10.5, 10.5 - 11.25, respectively, across four proto-clusters. Notably, the two GOODS-N proto-clusters at z=4.406 and z=5.194 have a quiescent fraction of 100% (2/2 at z=4.406; 1/1 at z=5.194) in their highest mass bin (log(M*/Msun) > 10.5), whereas the proto-clusters in GOODS-S at similar redshifts have zero massive quiescent galaxies. Contrary to the expectation that massive galaxies occupy cluster centers at z~0, our QGs are found primarily on the outskirts of overdensity peaks. We also find fewer robust QGs at z>5 (1/8) and none in the z=5.384 proto-cluster, consistent with simulations suggesting that efficient quenching mechanisms had not yet matured. Our results highlight the pronounced variations in quiescent fractions across proto-clusters at z>4. The emerging diversity of proto-cluster QG populations calls for a stronger understanding of the role of environment in early galaxy evolution.
comments: Submitted to ApJ. 21 pages, 11 figures, 5 tables

figs.cap: Photometric redshift distribution of sources around the proto-cluster at $z_{od}=4.267$ in GOODS-S. A prominent peak is visible and fitted with a Gaussian plus continuum model. The total fit is shown as a blue curve, whereas the gray line shows the continuum. The center of the Gaussian fit is defined as the redshift of the proto-cluster $z_{od}=4.267$ (red dashed line). The quiescent region (black dashed line) is adopted from Belli et al. [8]. We modify the selection to Equation 4 (black solid line) to include young, rare high-redshift quiescent galaxies. [1] to Equation 7 (diagonal solid black line) to include younger quiescent galaxies. Lastly, the bottom panels correspond to the GMM/NUVU$-$VJ selection from Gould et al. [36]. Gray background histograms show the distribution of all galaxies in our photometric catalogs. See Sections III.4.1, III.4.2, and III.4.3 for more details about each selection method.

The robust quiescent galaxies are shown as magenta stars. Other quiescent candidates are shown as cyan square. In the $z=4.406$ proto-cluster (left), the proto-cluster members include H$\alpha$ emitting galaxies with spectroscopic redshifts at $4.3<z_{\rm spec}<4.5$ [25] in orange and galaxies with photometric redshifts $4.2<z_{phot}<4.7$ in gray. We also highlight the sub-structures defined in Herard-Demanche et al. [41] in varying color dots (red, blue, green, dim gray, purple, light blue, lawn green, and olive). The overlaid contour lines and color bar represent the spatial galaxy number overdensity contrast, defined as: $\delta_{\rm gal}=(\rho/\rho_{\rm field})-1$, where $\rho$ is the local surface density computed via a Gaussian Kernel Density Estimate (KDE) and $\rho_{\rm field}$ is the average background number density across the FRESCO survey area. The color bar scales logarithmically and begins at $\delta_{\rm gal}=0.1$, representing regions 10% overdense relative to the field. The high-contrast regions trace the peaks of the overdensities. The gray shaded region in the background marks the coverage of FRESCO in GOODS-N.

title: Impact of Neutrino Trapping on the Equation of State and Structure of Hybrid Stars with 2SC Quark Matter
authors: Andrea Sabatucci, Armen Sedrakian
abstract: We investigate how sensitive the effects of neutrino trapping on hot hybrid stars are to uncertainties in the hadronic and quark equations of state and in the thermodynamic construction of the hadron--quark transition. The hadronic phase is described by finite-temperature covariant density functional equations of state, and the quark phase by a three-flavor Nambu--Jona-Lasinio (NJL) model with repulsive vector interactions and two-flavor color superconductivity. Because confinement is absent from the NJL model, an effective pressure shift $B^*$ is used phenomenologically to locate the deconfinement transition. We construct isentropic stellar equations of state with and without trapped electron neutrinos, vary the quark vector coupling and the nuclear symmetry-energy slope, and compare global with local conservation of electron-lepton number within phase coexistence. Neutrino trapping generically shifts deconfinement toward higher density throughout the parameter range considered. Increasing the vector interaction stiffens quark matter and raises the maximum stellar mass, but only moderately for the couplings studied. We also examine stronger diquark pairing and RG-consistent regularization, instead of sharp momentum cut-off: both affect the pairing gap, phase boundaries, and quark-core composition more strongly than they alter the qualitative trends of the stellar mass--radius sequences. Conversely, trapping reduces the sensitivity to the hadronic symmetry-energy slope because the enhanced proton fraction drives matter toward greater isospin symmetry. Global and local lepton-number prescriptions produce rather similar mass--radius relations but substantially different internal phase structures: global conservation leads to a considerably more extended mixed phase.

figs.cap: Difference $\Delta P=P_{Q}-P_{H}$ between the quark- and hadronic-matter pressures as a function of the baryon chemical potential for three values of the effective pressure shift $B^{*}$. The solid and dashed curves are evaluated for neutrino-transparent matter at $T=2$ and $60$ MeV, respectively, as indicated in the plot. Regions with $\Delta P<0$ favor hadronic matter, whereas $\Delta P>0$ favors quark matter. The zeros of $\Delta P$ identify the mechanical coexistence points and illustrate how the phenomenological parameter $B^{*}$ controls the effective location of the deconfinement transition. With the convention $P_{Q}=P_{Q}^{(0)}-B^{*}$, a more negative $B^{*}$ raises $P_{Q}$ and shifts its crossing with the hadronic pressure.

Projection of the phase-equilibrium construction onto the $(\mu_{B},\mu_{Le})$ plane for the reference model at $Y_{Le}=0.4$. The trajectories corresponding to locally charge-neutral hadronic and quark matter are shown together with the coexistence line obtained from the generalized Gibbs conditions. The filled circles indicate the entrance into and exit from the mixed phase. For each phase, lighter shades correspond to lower temperatures.

Mass–radius relations for isentropic hybrid stars obtained for different values of the vector coupling $\eta_{V}$. Increasing the repulsive vector interaction stiffens the quark-matter equation of state and produces a moderate increase of the maximum stellar mass.

Internal profiles of maximum-mass isentropic hybrid-star configurations with trapped electron neutrinos ($Y_{Le}=0.4$). The left and right panels correspond to $S=1$ and $S=2$, respectively. The upper panels show the Gibbs construction with globally conserved electron-lepton number, while the lower panels show the Maxwell construction with a locally fixed lepton fraction. Shading indicates pure quark, mixed, and hadronic regions. Although the global stellar properties are similar, the Gibbs construction produces a substantially more extended mixed-phase region.

Mass–radius sequences for lepton-rich isentropic hybrid stars with $Y_{Le}=0.4$, $\eta_{D}=1.25$, and $\eta_{V}=0.8,1.0,1.2$. The left and right panels show $S=1$ and $S=2$, respectively. Dots identify the maximum masses along the displayed sequences.

Mass–radius sequences at fixed phenomenological pressure shift $B^{*}$ for $\eta_{V}=0.8,1.0,1.2$, with trapped electron neutrinos ($Y_{Le}=0.4$). The upper row uses $\eta_{D}=1$ and $B^{*}=-15\,\mathrm{MeV\,fm^{-3}}$; the lower row uses $\eta_{D}=1.25$ and $B^{*}=-5\,\mathrm{MeV\,fm^{-3}}$. The left and right panels in each row correspond to $S=1$ and $S=2$. Compare with Figs. 6 and 12, where $B^{*}$ is readjusted separately for each $\eta_{V}$ according to the prescription in Sec. V.2. In both comparisons, larger vector repulsion supports larger maximum masses.

title: The CGM in a New Light: Emitted H$α$, [NII], and [OIII] around Simulated Dwarf Galaxies
authors: Daniel R. Piacitelli, Alyson M. Brooks, N. Nicole Sanchez, Charlotte Christensen, Chloe Neufeld, Imad Pasha, Pieter van Dokkum, Akaxia Cruz, Ben Keller, Thomas R. Quinn, Sijing Shen, James Wadsley
abstract: Mapping the circumgalactic medium (CGM) in emission is a critical next step in understanding its role in the baryon cycle and galaxy evolution, and dwarf galaxies ($M_{\star}\lesssim 10^9 M_{\odot}$) are essential laboratories to study the effects of feedback on the CGM. Using the Marvelous Massive Dwarfs simulation suite, we model the CGM surface brightness (SB) around dwarf galaxies in H$\alpha$, [NII]$\lambda$6583, and [OIII]$\lambda$5007, lines accessible to current integral-field spectrographs (e.g., MUSE and KCWI) and to narrow-band imaging with the MOTHRA telephoto array. We investigate trends in SB magnitude, extent, and geometry as well as correlations with gas kinematics, recent star formation, and galaxy size. Emission in the three lines typically traces distinct CGM structures and phases. SB and the size of the emitting region can differ significantly at a given galaxy mass, but enhancements or suppression in either brightness or extent correlate well across lines. Typically, emission is preferentially eccentric and oriented along the galaxy's semi-minor axis. While outflows are key drivers in dispersing metals into the CGM and shaping SB, they remain difficult to identify in SB maps and contribute $\sim40\%$ of the total SB across lines and galaxy masses, while inflows contribute $\sim50\%$. Finally, we identify evidence for a positive correlation between SB and recent star formation and weaker but still significant evidence for a negative correlation between SB and HI disk size. These results link CGM emission to both a galaxy's recent star formation and its cumulative evolution, yielding predictions that ongoing surveys can test and further establishing emission mapping as a new window into the baryon cycle.
comments: 22 pages, 14 figures

figs.cap: Surface brightness (SB) maps in H$\alpha$ (left), [N ii] (center), and [O iii] (right) for four representative galaxies at $z=0$, oriented edge-on based on the angular momentum vector. The top two rows show two $\log M_{\star}/M_{\odot}\sim 9$ galaxies and the bottom two rows show two representative $\log M_{\star}/M_{\odot}\sim 8$ galaxies; both mass bins include a disky and non-disky galaxy to showcase how galaxy morphology may shape CGM SB. For reference, we include contours describing the size of the disk/halo: the $B$-band stellar SB brighter than $\mu_{B}=27.5\rm\,mag~arcsec^{-2}$ (yellow), HI surface density above $\Sigma_{\rm HI}=1\rm\,M_{\odot}~pc^{-2}$ (black), and $0.5\ R_{\rm vir}$ and $1\ R_{\rm vir}$ (dotted white circles) are overplotted on each map. The solid white contours are SB contours at $10^{-20}$ $\rm{erg\,s^{-1}\,cm^{-2}\,arcsec^{-2}}$and $10^{-22}$ $\rm{erg\,s^{-1}\,cm^{-2}\,arcsec^{-2}}$, the approximate expected threshold for MOTHRA observations is $2\times 10^{-21}$ $\rm{erg\,s^{-1}\,cm^{-2}\,arcsec^{-2}}$. We find that observable SB in all three lines extends well into the CGM, with each line tracing differing structures.

Top row: Median $\log\,\rm SB$ each galaxy within $0.5R_{\rm vir}$ in H$\alpha$ (left), [N ii$]\lambda$6583 (center), and [O iii$]\lambda$5007 (right). Error bars denote $16-84\rm th$ percentile ranges for the SB values in each map. Bottom row: Total luminosity (in $\log\rm erg\ s^{-1}$) in each line for particles within a spherical region with radius $r=0.5R_{\rm vir}$. We plot power-law fits of $\log\rm{SB}\,$ for the high-mass and low-mass samples and provide the slopes in each panel. Shaded regions correspond to the $1\sigma$ and $2\sigma$ scatter of the computed $\log\rm{SB}$ about the fit line. Generally, the brightness of metal lines falls off more steeply with declining stellar mass than H$\alpha$.

Halo covering fractions above a fixed SB threshold of $10^{-20}$ $\rm{erg\,s^{-1}\,cm^{-2}\,arcsec^{-2}}$ (light blue markers) and $10^{-22}$ $\rm{erg\,s^{-1}\,cm^{-2}\,arcsec^{-2}}$ (black markers) for H$\alpha$ (left), [N ii$]\lambda$6583 (center), and [O iii$]\lambda$5007 (right). Covering fractions for each galaxy are shown with respect to stellar mass. We derive these values by calculating the total area enclosed by the SB contour at the chosen threshold, then dividing by the total halo area. To account for viewing-angle variations, we orient the galaxy edge-on and then rotate it from edge-on to face-on through $30$ evenly spaced viewing angles, deriving the covering fraction for each angle. Plotted markers denote the mean covering fraction over all viewing angles, while the error bars represent the minimum to maximum. For reference of physical scale, orange lines and bands are included that represent the fractional size of a $r=10,\ 30,\ 60\rm\ kpc$ halo relative to the mean $R_{\rm vir}$ at that stellar mass. Galaxies with mean bright covering fractions below $0.6\%$ (2 in [N ii], 17 in [O iii], all with $M_{\star}<10^{8.1}M_{\odot}$) are shown as open-faced upper limits at the bottom of each panel. H$\alpha$-emitting regions are typically comparable or larger in covering fractions compared to [N ii] and [O iii] for both SB thresholds.

SB maps of a representative $\log M_{\star}/M_{\odot}\sim 9$ galaxy split into inflows (upper row) and outflows (bottom row). These SB maps are made by first selecting only inflowing ($v_{r}<-0.1v_{\rm vir}$) and outflowing ($v_{r}>0.1v_{\rm vir}$) particles, then using the same SB map pipeline as Figure 2. White dotted contours show $0.5R_{\rm vir}$ and $R_{\rm vir}$.

SB correlations with SFR. SB residuals (presented in Figure 4) are plotted on the horizontal axis, and SFR residuals ($\Delta\log\rm{SFR}$, derived from Figure 1) are plotted on the vertical axis. Linear regression fits and uncertainties are shown as grey dashed lines and shaded bands and slopes with uncertainties are reported in the top-left corner. Pearson correlation coefficients (r) are shown in the bottom-left corners. Correlations are computed for the full plotted sample, and the reported correlation ranges are computed via jackknifing. The range of minimum to maximum correlations from the jackknifing procedure is reported in the bottom-left corner. Across lines, we find significant ($r>0.5$) correlations between the SB and recent SFR. This correlation tends to be stronger for H$\alpha$ SB than [O iii] SB and [N ii] SB. Generally, these correlations imply that the CGM tends to be brighter at a given mass for galaxies with enhanced SFRs.

Top panel: Median metallicity relative to solar ($Z/Z_{\odot}$) of all gas within $0.5R_{\rm vir}$ versus stellar mass. All markers across panels are color-coded by $R_{\rm HI}$ residuals. Error bars show the standard deviation of particle data of the selected region. Middle panel: Fraction of metals retained. This quantity is found by dividing the total oxygen mass for all gas mass within $R_{\rm vir}$ by the total oxygen mass produced over the galaxy’s SFH, following Piacitelli et al. [45]. Bottom panel: Total gas mass within $R_{\rm vir}$ divided by $M_{\rm vir}$. We find that compact galaxies ($\Delta{\text{$R_{\rm HI}$}}<0$ pink markers) tend to have higher metallicity CGM, leading to the enhanced SB seen in Figure 13. These compact galaxies also have lower metal retention rates and lower gas fractions, indicating that these galaxies experience more efficient feedback that pushes metals and gas beyond the halo, compared to more extended galaxies.

title: A Point-source Catalogue from Direction-dependent Calibrated 21CMA Images
authors: Qizhe Tang, Jingying Wang, Junhua Gu, Qian Zheng, Quan Guo, Tingyan Shen, Bixuan Zhao, Qiuyi Lai, Yan Huang, Kuanjun Li, Yang Feng
abstract: We present a deep low-frequency radio point-source catalogue centred on the North Celestial Pole (NCP) and extending $5^\circ$ in radius, derived from a single 24-h observation with the 21 CentiMeter Array (21CMA). Covering 75-175 MHz, the catalogue characterises extragalactic foreground point sources for Epoch of Reionization (EoR) studies. Previous 21CMA imaging has been limited by reduced dynamic range caused by direction-dependent effects, particularly the severe grating lobes of ultra-bright sources such as 3C 61.1 and ionospheric phase distortions. Here we apply 21CMAcali, a direction-dependent calibration and imaging pipeline, to mitigate these effects. The angular resolution ranges from 2.3 arcmin at 100 MHz to 1.4 arcmin at 168.75 MHz. The resulting maps show reduced artefacts and background noise, enabling more reliable recovery of faint sources. We construct a catalogue of 1246 radio point sources. Cross-matching with LoTSS-DR3, WENSS, and NVSS enables broad-band spectral fitting, while an independent in-band analysis yields a median spectral index of $\alpha=-0.825$ (where $S \propto \nu^{\alpha}$). The Euclidean-normalised differential source counts at 150 MHz, derived from a dedicated 50-MHz-wide multi-frequency synthesis (MFS) image, are broadly consistent with existing measurements and semi-empirical models at the bright end, whereas the deficit at lower flux densities ($S \lesssim 0.04$ Jy) mainly reflects limited sensitivity and incompleteness. This catalogue improves foreground point-source characterisation in the 21CMA NCP field, demonstrates the value of direction-dependent calibration, and provides a reference for deeper catalogues based on multi-day observations.
comments: 22 pages, 19 figures, 7 tables. Accepted for publication in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society (MNRAS)

The colour bar shows the brightness temperature in K. The white cross marks the NCP, and the red dashed circle indicates the core target region ($\mathrm{Dec}>85^{\circ}$) in this work.

The small cross marks the beam centre, corresponding to the NCP pointing direction.

Blue dots represent the 611 sources detected in both catalogues. Open dark green circles mark the 13 sources appearing only in Z2016, while orange dots indicate the 635 sources newly identified in 21CMA-DDR1.

Distributions of the integrated flux densities of the 580 real point sources detected within the central $3^{\circ}$ core region ($\mathrm{Dec}>87^{\circ}$). In each panel, the shaded histogram (left axis) shows the absolute number of sources in each logarithmic flux-density bin, while the solid line with square markers (right axis) gives the cumulative number of sources.

The simulations were restricted to the central $3^{\circ}$ core region ($\mathrm{Dec}>87^{\circ}$). The solid lines with circles show the mean completeness from 500 independent realisations, while the shaded regions indicate the corresponding $1\sigma$ standard deviations.

The red squares represent the source counts derived from the dedicated 21CMA 150 MHz wide-band MFS image within the central $3^{\circ}$ core region ($\mathrm{Dec}>87^{\circ}$). For comparison, representative literature measurements are also shown, namely the LOFAR Deep Fields (grey downward triangles; Mandal et al. 2021), LOFAR Boötes (blue circles; Williams et al. 2016), and MWA GLEAM (green upward triangles; Franzen et al. 2019). The cyan dotted and orange dashed curves denote the predictions of the SKADS (Wilman et al., 2008) and T-RECS (Bonaldi et al., 2019) simulation models, respectively.

title: Cosmological constraints on single-field inflation models from ACT/SPT data and observations at sub-Mpc scales
authors: Qing-Yang Wang, Jing-Zhi Zhou, Fei-Yu Chen, Zhi-Chao Li
abstract: We investigate single-field inflation models that can produce large curvature perturbations at sub-Mpc scales while remaining consistent with cosmological observations across multiple regimes. We highlight the tension between generating enhanced small-scale perturbations and maintaining agreement with the scalar spectral index $n_s$ measured by ACT and SPT, which disfavors several conventional single-field inflation models. To address this issue, we propose three viable classes of inflationary potentials: bump/dip-modified, step-like, and double-inflection-point. Each can sufficiently amplify primordial perturbations while predicting $n_s$ that lie within the $2\sigma$ range of current observational bounds. In addition, we examine the primordial power spectra predicted by these models and constrain their parameter spaces using cosmological observations at different scales, including CMB, BAO, PBH, PTA, and CMB-distortion. Our results show that some of the models considered can simultaneously satisfy the ACT/SPT constraints and account for the current PTA observations, although doing so while respecting the constraints on the PBH abundance remains challenging.
comments: 17 pages, 5 figures

figs.cap: Inflation potentials (upper panels) and curvature perturbation spectra $\mathcal{P}_{\zeta}(k)$ (lower panels) for three inflation models. Left: the bump/dip-modified KKLT model with $M=1$, $n=1$, $V_{0}=3.9\times 10^{-10}M_{P}^{4}$, $\phi_{0}=3.98M_{P}$ fixed; solid (dashed) lines correspond to positive (negative) feature amplitude $A$, and the inset zooms into the bump/dip region of the potential. Middle: the step-modified Starobinsky model with $V_{0}=5\times 10^{-11}M_{P}^{4}$, $n=3$, $\sigma=10^{3}$, $\phi_{0}=5$, $d=0.2$ fixed; the rapid oscillations of the spectra around the peak are physical and are shown without any smoothing. Right: the double-inflection-point model with $\Lambda=1$, $V_{0}=5.7\times 10^{-12}M_{P}^{4}$, $\phi_{1}=1.437$, $\phi_{2}=6$, $b_{2}=0$, $b_{6}=-10^{-3}$ fixed; the inset zooms into the ultra-slow-roll dip of the potential.

Present-day energy-density spectra $h^{2}\bar{\Omega}_{\mathrm{GW},0}^{(2)}(k)$ of the \tl_set:NeSIGW produced by the enhanced primordial spectra of the three inflation models, for the same parameter sets as in Fig. 1. Left: bump/dip-modified KKLT model. Middle: step-modified Starobinsky model; the thin light curves are computed from the raw oscillatory primordial spectra, while the thick curves use the oscillation-averaged spectra (arithmetic average over a $0.1$ dex window in $\ln k$). Right: double-inflection-point model. The shaded vertical band marks the \tl_set:NePTA-sensitive range.

Observational constraints on the parameter spaces of the three inflation models. (a) Bump/dip-modified KKLT model with $\sigma=0.02$, shown in the $(\phi_{0},\,\delta)$ plane with $\delta\equiv 1-|A|/|A_{\max}|$ for the bump ($A>0$, left) and dip ($A<0$, right) cases; (b) step-modified Starobinsky model with $n=3$, $\sigma=10^{3}$, $d=0.2$, shown in the $(\phi_{0},\,A)$ plane; (c) double-inflection-point model, shown in the $(b_{3},\,\delta)$ plane with $\delta\equiv|b_{5}|/|b_{5}^{\max}|-1$. In every panel the light-green region labeled “allowed” satisfies all the constraints considered in this work. The colored regions are excluded: red by the \tl_set:NePBH abundance ($f_{\mathrm{pbh}}>1$); blue by the \tl_set:NeCMB$+$\tl_set:NeBAO bound on the total \tl_set:NeSIGW energy density, Eq. (32); orange and purple by the COBE/FIRAS $\mu$- and $y$-distortion bounds, Eq. (36), respectively. In panel (c) the dark-gray region is excluded because the inflaton is trapped in the ultra-slow-roll dip and cannot reach the potential minimum ($|b_{5}|>|b_{5}^{\max}|$). In panel (b) the \tl_set:NePBH, \tl_set:NeSIGW, and $y$-distortion constraints are all weaker than the $\mu$-distortion bound and do not appear. The dotted gray contours mark the peak scale $k_{p}=10^{4},\,10^{6},\,10^{8}\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}$ of the primordial power spectrum. All distortion constraints are evaluated with the raw (unsmoothed) primordial spectra.

Posterior distributions of the model parameters from the Bayesian analysis of the NANOGrav 15-year data set, assuming that \tl_set:NeSIGW dominate the \tl_set:NePTA signal. (a) The bump/dip-modified KKLT model in $(A,\phi_{0})$, with the bump ($A>0$, left) and dip ($A<0$, right) cases shown separately; (b) the step-modified Starobinsky model in $(A,\phi_{0})$; (c) the double-inflection-point model in $(b_{5},b_{3})$. The dark and light green regions denote the $68\%$ and $95\%$ credible regions, and the dashed lines mark the one-dimensional medians. The well-localized, strongly degenerate posteriors of the KKLT and double-inflection-point models contrast with the diffuse, prior-dominated posterior of the step model, the latter reflecting the poor fit of its \tl_set:NeSIGW spectrum to the data.

The $68\%$ and $95\%$ credible regions of the NANOGrav 15-year posteriors (dark and light green contours, with the posterior median marked by the cross) overlaid on the constraint maps: (a) the bump/dip-modified KKLT model in the $(\phi_{0},\delta)$ plane, with the bump ($A>0$, left) and dip ($A<0$, right) cases shown separately; (b) the step-modified Starobinsky model in the $(\phi_{0},A)$ plane; (c) the double-inflection-point model in the $(b_{3},\delta)$ plane. The excluded regions follow the same convention as Fig. 3. For both KKLT cases the \tl_set:NePTA-favored region is pinned to the near-critical edge $\delta\rightarrow 0$ and lies almost entirely inside the \tl_set:NePBH-excluded region. For the step model the posterior lies inside the allowed region, but the corresponding \tl_set:NeSIGW spectra do not fit the NANOGrav data, see Table 1. For the double-inflection-point model the bulk of the posterior overlaps the \tl_set:NePBH-excluded region, while a subdominant tail at $b_{3}\gtrsim 4.65\times 10^{-4}$ survives inside the allowed band.

title: The Clouds in the "Middle Ages" I. Star formation history and chemical abundances in the LMC
authors: Mathias Schultheis, Maria-Rosa L. Cioni, Samuele Anoardo
abstract: The LMC is a benchmark galaxy for studying stellar evolution, chemical enrichment, and galaxy interactions due to its proximity and intermediate metallicity. While its star formation history (SFH) has been extensively studied using colour-magnitude diagram (CMD) fitting techniques and the chemical enrichment is largely based on red giant branch (RGB) stars, the asymptotic giant branch (AGB) population - a key tracer of intermediate-ages - has received less attention in these analyses. We aim to reconstruct the SFH of the LMC using AGB stars and to study their reliability as tracers of chemical abundances. The initial sample of 879 AGB stars from the Gaia DR3 long-period variable catalog was extended to 2047 fundamental-mode pulsators by applying separate O-rich and C-rich period-Wesenheit relations; OGLE-III cross-matching then showed that only 256 of these stars are Mira variables. We reconstructed the SFH using two period-age calibrations: the theoretical relation of Trabucchi and Mowlavi (2022) and the empirical calibration of Zhang and Sanders (2023). For the chemical abundance analysis, we used APOGEE DR17 spectra for 296 AGB and 271 RGB stars, applying a refined line-by-line abundance pipeline with a tailored line selection to derive Mg, Si, and Ca abundances. The two calibrations yield significantly different SFHs, and neither matches independent CMD-based results equally well, so we present both rather than one fiducial choice. Our SFH reveals three distinct phases: an ancient population at 9-10 Gyr, a quiescent phase at 4-8 Gyr, and a starburst peaking at 1.5-2 Gyr. Our chemical analysis demonstrates that carefully selected Mg, Si, and Ca lines yield significantly reduced intrinsic scatter compared to APOGEE DR17 results. AGB stars prove to be reliable tracers of both the SFH and chemical enrichment of the LMC, provided that careful line selection and calibration are applied.
comments: 13 pages, 13 figures, accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics

figs.cap: LMC sample of the LPV Gaia DR3 catalog (Lebzelter et al. 2023). title: Probing the inner disk edge of rotating neutron stars with dipole excitations in finite nuclei
authors: P.S. Koliogiannis, N. Paar
abstract: The nuclear equation of state shapes both the structure of rapidly rotating neutron stars and the orbital motion in their surrounding spacetime. Its uncertainty affects the mass and radius at which the innermost stable circular orbit reaches the stellar surface, a condition that defines the transition between disks whose inner edge is set by the surface and those truncated by orbital instability. We quantify how measurements of the electric dipole polarizability of neutron-rich nuclei reduce the uncertainty in this transition and in the orbital properties at the disk inner edge. We compute uniformly rotating neutron stars in general relativity for a family of equations of state that systematically vary the symmetry energy, derived from relativistic energy density functionals with density-dependent point-coupling interactions. We compare the results for the full family with those for the subset consistent with the measured dipole polarizabilities of finite nuclei. The dipole polarizability constraint reduces the spread in transition mass and equatorial radius by factors of about seven to ten across the spin frequencies considered. Along this transition, it also confines the orbital frequency at the disk inner edge to a band narrower than $20$~Hz at each spin. Combined with a measured neutron-star spin, a kilohertz quasi-periodic oscillation interpreted as disk orbital motion further restricts the mass--radius region, allowing an independent mass estimate to probe the symmetry-energy constraint. The dipole response of finite nuclei thus informs both the structure of rotating neutron stars and the orbital properties of their inner accretion disks.
comments: 4 pages, 3 figures

title: The dearth of dustless HdC stars in the Magellanic Clouds: A metallicity-driven white dwarf merger mass effect
authors: Patrick Tisserand, Ashley J. Ruiter, Eden Cheng, Jamie Soon, Anais Möller, Courtney L. Crawford, George Bowden, Ivo R. Seitenzahl, Simon J. Murphy, Christopher A. Onken, Christian Wolf, Geoffrey C. Clayton
abstract: Hydrogen-deficient carbon (HdC) stars are rare supergiants believed to form through the merger of two white dwarfs (WDs). They comprise the dust-producing R Coronae Borealis (RCB) stars and the dustless HdC (dLHdC) stars. While dedicated Galactic surveys find the two subclasses in roughly equal numbers, no dLHdC star had previously been identified in the Magellanic Clouds, despite 30 known RCB stars in these two galaxies. We present the first systematic search for dLHdC stars in the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds, aiming to measure the dLHdC-to-RCB ratio in environments of distinct metallicities and well-constrained star formation histories. Candidates were selected from the Gaia DR3 Magellanic catalogue using colour-magnitude cuts combining Gaia, SkyMapper DR4, and VMC DR6 photometry, complemented by a random-forest classifier trained on known Galactic dLHdC stars. The search reached an overall detection efficiency of ~96%. All candidates were followed up spectroscopically with WiFeS on the ANU 2.3m telescope. We discovered the first two Magellanic dLHdC stars: SP77 29-5 in the LMC and SMSS 005551.43-723139.2 in the SMC, the latter belonging to the rare Sr-rich subclass. The resulting dLHdC-to-RCB number ratio of ~1:15 overall is far below the near-unity Galactic value. We argue this deficit is intrinsic rather than observational. Convolving the delay time distribution from a sub-class of white dwarf mergers with each Cloud's star formation history, we estimate that ~80% (LMC) and about two-thirds (SMC) of HdC stars originate from mergers with short delay times, which at low metallicity are biased towards higher total WD masses, and thus towards the luminous regime associated with RCB stars rather than the fainter dLHdC population.
comments: 17 pages, 20 figures. Accepted for publication in A&A

title: Evidence for a nova super-remnant surrounding the recurrent nova V745 Scorpii using eROSITA
authors: Michael W. Healy-Kalesh, Sara Saeedi, Manami Sasaki, Matthew J. Darnley, Michael M. Shara, Werner Becker, Martin G. F. Mayer, Federico Zangrandi
abstract: Nova super-remnants (NSRs) are vast shell-like structures encompassing recurrent novae (RNe), created through the excavation of large amounts of local interstellar medium by repeated nova eruptions. Simulations predict that such NSRs should surround all novae. Indeed, NSRs have now been discovered around the Galactic RNe KT Eridani, RS Ophiuchi and T Coronae Borealis, and the Large Magellanic Cloud RN LMCN 1971-08a, to place alongside the prototypical NSR in M31, associated with the extreme RN, M31N 2008-12a. Highly energetic novae ejecta impacting the inner boundary of the NSR shell alongside inter-ejecta shocks are predicted to generate high levels of X-ray emission in the form of an extended shell-like structure. A search for X-ray emission from a present NSR surrounding the Galactic RN, V745 Scorpii, using observations from the extended Roentgen Survey with an Imaging Telescope Array (eROSITA) on board Spektrum-Roentgen-Gamma (Spektr-RG, SRG) led to the identification of a shell coincident with the nova. Based on (i) the structure being aligned with the location of the central nova; (ii) its size being consistent with the sizes of other known NSRs; (iii) the similarity between the emission radial profiles of the X-ray structure and the confirmed NSR around M31N 2008-12a; (vi) the presence of a corresponding infrared cavity; (v) the resemblance of the radial profile of the synthetic X-ray ring derived from a modelled NSR structure with the radial profile of the observed ring; and (vi) the lack of other sources capable of creating such a large structure, we propose this X-ray structure to be another Galactic NSR to be uncovered, and the first NSR to be captured through its X-ray emission.
comments: 13 pages, 10 figures; Accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics

title: Getting Ready For Analysing Rubin Data : CLMM v2, The Updated LSST-DESC Cluster Weak Lensing Mass Modeling Library For Cosmology
authors: Michel Aguena, Céline Combet, Shenming Fu, Constantin Payerne, Marina Ricci, Camille Avestruz, Eduardo Barroso, de Oliveira Caio, Zhou Conghao, Hsin Fan, Calum Murray, Anna Niemiec, Nikolina Sarcevic, Tae-hyeon Shin, Rance Solomon, Radhakrishnan Srinivasan, Sunayama Tomomi, Yuanyuan Zhang, Joe Zuntz
abstract: The Dark Energy Science Collaboration has prepared a multitude of pipelines to process the upcoming Vera C. Rubin Observatory data and perform different scientific analyses. Here, we present the methodology to constrain the mass information of galaxy clusters from weak lensing, which is encompassed by the v2.0 release of the Cluster Lensing Mass Modeling (CLMM) code. This Python library provides the ingredients for both the modeling and data reduction of lensing observables, and the improvements in the new version were customized to handle the first WL analyses of LSST clusters, including, e.g., stacking functionalities and WL multipoles. This new version of CLMM has allowed various cluster analyses using LSST-DESC simulated data, precursor survey and Rubin commissioning and survey validation data, and is ready to be used for the first cluster cosmology analyses. CLMM is an open-source software package collaboratively written in Python, providing multiple example notebooks, including a set that can reproduce all figures in this work, and extensive documentation, publicly available at this https URL.
comments: 10 pages, 12 figures

title: How common are extreme scattering events?: First large sample from the ASKAP VAST survey
authors: Akash Anumarlapudi, Dylan L. Jow, Artem Tuntsov, Hayley Bignall, David L. Kaplan, Dougal Dobie, B. M. Gaensler, Igor L. Andreoni, Laura Driessen, Tara Murphy, Joshua Pritchard
abstract: Compact radio sources are occasionally observed to undergo extreme scattering events (ESEs): large, chromatic flux-density variations, often by more than a factor of two, over a few months. These were interpreted to be a smooth plasma lensing phenomenon due to AU-scale structures in the ISM. Although ESEs were discovered decades ago, observationally, only a few tens of ESEs have been reported, often from individual sources monitored at very high cadences. As such, the nature of the plasma lenses generating such events remains elusive. In this article, we present the most comprehensive sample of ESEs to date, using the ASKAP Variables and Slow Transients (VAST) survey. We report the discovery of a three-tier sample --- 72 sources that show promising ESE events (gold), 76 sources that are likely ESE-exhibiting (silver), and an additional 88 sources where ESE events are one plausible explanation (bronze). We show that the light curves demonstrate varied morphologies, which can be interpreted in terms of the source size and the strength of the lens in the paradigm of a simple one-dimensional Gaussian lens model. The spatial distribution of ESEs shows an appreciable excess in the direction of the Galactic center and along the Galactic loops. Using this sample, we infer an overall rate of 0.012 such events per year per deg^2 (or 0.006 events per source per year) for our (gold+silver) sample, for sources with mean flux density above 5 mJy at 888 MHz (0.01% of all isolated point sources detected in VAST).
comments: Under review in The Astrophysical Journal, any comments are welcome

title: Neglecting Dynamical Microlensing Can Bias Accretion Disk Size Measurements at the Population Level
authors: Joshua Fagin, James Hung-Hsu Chan, Connor Stone, Henry Best, Paras Sharma, Sophia Miskiewicz, Matthew O'Dowd, Laurence Perreault-Levasseur, Yashar Hezaveh, Simon Birrer
abstract: Microlensing of strongly lensed quasars probes unresolved accretion disks, but many inference methods use static magnification maps with fixed relative microlens positions. Using the GPU-accelerated simulator Microcaustics, we generate ten-year multiband light curves for three quadruply lensed quasar configurations. We compare dynamical microlensing with independent microlens motions against coherent bulk motion, and a microlens mass distribution against equal masses, keeping the velocity distribution of individual microlenses and mean mass fixed. We infer population disk sizes using ridge regression on the means and lower and upper scatters of ten variability and event metrics. We measure biases by applying models trained with simplified physics to simulations including both effects. Models trained on coherent motion interpret the additional variability from evolving caustics as smaller disks. For populations of 128 independent realizations, jointly inferred radii are consistently smaller by 6-28%. Microlens dynamics increase caustic-crossing rates pooled across all four macroimages by 5-15% and r-band high-magnification-event (HME) rates by 13-25%, while shortening median HME durations by 4-12%. Omitting the mass distribution produces configuration-dependent disk-size offsets from -12% to +5%. Including the mass distribution decreases caustic-crossing rates by 6-8% and HME rates by 6-12%. It also narrows the spread of ten-year averaged microlensing time-delay differences between macroimages by a median of 9-12% per system, while microlens dynamics have a smaller, image-pair-dependent effect. These results demonstrate the importance of microlens dynamics for population disk-size inference and motivate simulations that include dynamical microlensing and a microlens mass distribution.

title: Variable Stars in Local Group Galaxies IX: Tracing the Complex History of NGC 205
authors: Irina Plaks, M. Marengo, M. Monelli, C. R. Kerton, Giuliana Fiorentino, G. Bono, Clara E. Martínez-Vázquez
abstract: We present the most extensive catalogue of variable stars in NGC 205 to date, based on archival HST/ACS imaging of a single field $\sim 4^\prime$ from the galaxy centre (GO-15902). We detect 1441 RR Lyrae stars (1064 RRab, 363 RRc, and 14 of uncertain mode) and 35 anomalous Cepheids, and measure their periods, amplitudes, and intensity-mean magnitudes in the F606W and F814W bands. The variable population is dominated by RR Lyrae stars, as expected for a predominantly old (>10 Gyr) field with no strong young component. From the red giant branch tip we derive a distance modulus of $\mu = 24.68 \pm 0.06$ mag. The distribution of the RR Lyrae stars in the Bailey diagram, the fraction of RRc stars, and the presence of a substantial population of high-amplitude short-period RRab stars, indicate a range of metallicities extending to a metal-rich component, while the ratio of RR Lyrae stars to red giant branch stars indicates an extended star formation history, with only a modest fraction of the stellar mass formed in the first few Gyr. The anomalous Cepheids place NGC 205 among the slow evolvers on the relation between their frequency and host luminosity, and comparison with evolutionary models constrains their progenitors to $[\mathrm{Fe/H}] \lesssim -2.1$, indicating that metal-poor gas remained available well after the galaxy had begun to enrich. In a forthcoming paper, we will use the RR Lyrae periods and intensity-mean magnitudes to derive individual metallicities for these stars and trace the chemical enrichment history of NGC 205.

figs.cap: Recovery of the simulated RRLs as a function of input period, F814W magnitude, and F606W amplitude, before (a) and after (b) alias removal. In each bin the stars are divided into those correctly recovered in both period and mode (green), those with the correct mode but a period more than 1 per cent from the input value (blue), and those counted as failed (red), comprising stars that did not pass the variability index cut and stars assigned the wrong mode. The alias-removal procedure improves recovery across the full range of all three parameters, with the largest improvements at short periods and low amplitudes.
