title: Absence of Magnetic Suppression in Massive Star Variability
authors: Linhao Ma, May G. Pedersen, Nicholas Z. Rui
abstract: Although stochastic low-frequency (SLF) variability is ubiquitous among hot, massive stars, its physical origin remains uncertain. One proposed explanation is that this variability is produced by internal gravity waves (IGWs) excited in the stellar interior by convection in the stellar core or subsurface layers. Strong magnetic fields, however, are expected to significantly attenuate such waves. In this work, we model the conditions for magnetic gravity-wave suppression in 17 magnetic hot stars that exhibit significant SLF variability. We find that in many cases, IGWs excited at frequencies comparable to the observed variability should be strongly suppressed by the magnetic field, sometimes across a substantial fraction of the frequency range containing the observed SLF power. This finding challenges IGWs as a universal explanation for SLF variability in massive stars and motivates the consideration of alternative origins.
comments: To submit to AAS Journals. Comments welcome!

figs.cap: Schematic of magnetic suppression of internal gravity waves (IGWs) in massive stars. Left: Without magnetic suppression and in the absence of other damping, IGWs can propagate through the radiative envelope and reach the stellar photosphere, appearing as SLF variability. Right: In stars with strong magnetic fields, the propagation of low-frequency IGWs is suppressed in the outer envelope as the density drops. The outward propagating gravity waves are converted into inward propagating magnetic waves (MWs), whose short wavelengths allow them to damp efficiently. Such magnetically suppressed gravity waves fail to reach the surface and cannot reproduce the observed SLF phenomenon.

Left: Asteroseismic propagation diagram for a $7.25\,M_{\odot}$ main-sequence model corresponding to the massive magnetic star HD 36485, which has a measured polar magnetic field $B_{\mathrm{p}}\approx 10\,\mathrm{kG}$. IGWs can propagate in the absence of a magnetic field in the gravity-mode region (blue shaded region) but are strongly magnetically damped when $\omega<\omega_{B}$ (red hatched region). The red dotted line indicates ${\nu_{\mathrm{supp}}}$, the linear frequency below which an IGW is magnetically suppressed before reaching the photosphere. Right: The observed power spectral density (PSD) for HD 36485 (black lines) and the total fractional integrated power (thick purple line) in the SLF frequency range. Roughly $51\%$ of power is below the magnetic suppression frequency, and were expected to be suppressed if they originated from IGWs that propagated from the stellar interior. The observed SLF variability in this star appears inconsistent with IGWs.

The expected suppressed power fraction and the strength of polar magnetic fields for the 17 magnetic stars in our analysis. The red dots show the estimates for dipole ($\ell=1$) IGWs, and the orange dots show the more conservative estimates excluding non-WKB waves. Overall, a substantial fraction of power are expected to be suppressed if they are from IGWs for many of the systems in our analysis. This questions the IGW interpretation as a common origin for stochastic low-frequency (SLF) variability.

Left: Propagating and evanescent regions for internal waves for the HD 36485 model in Figure 2. The blue and gray regions support the propagation of gravity and pressure waves. In the gold regions, waves are evanescent according to the standard non-magnetic gravito-acoustic (gp) dispersion relation and are attenuated by a factor $\exp(-2\int|\Im(k_{r,\mathrm{gp}})|\,dr)$, where $k_{r,\mathrm{gp}}$ is given by Equation 6. In the red regions, the waves are also evanescent, but due to magnetic suppression. The attenuation factor is instead given by $\exp(-2\int|\Im(k_{r,\mathrm{mg}})|\,dr)$, where $k_{r,\mathrm{mg}}$ is given by Equation 7. Right: The wave energy tunneling coefficient $T$ (solid black line) representing residual wave energy which survives evanescent decay from the propagating regions to the stellar surface. The small values of $T$ compared to the case without magnetic effects (dashed black line) validate our assumption that magneto-gravity waves damp out immediately upon reaching the magnetic suppression region.

Propagation diagram color-coded by $\log(|k_{r}H_{p}|)$ for the HD 36485 model shown in Figure 2 (left panel), with the power spectrum of HD 36485’s SLF variability reproduced in the right panel. Waves below $S_{1,\mathrm{WKB}}$ (dashed orange line) satisfy the WKB limit and experience magnetic suppression, while waves above this frequency experience a theoretically uncertain interaction with the magnetic field. Excluding physically uncertain non-WKB regions reduces ${
u_{\mathrm{supp}}}$ to a lower value $
u_{\mathrm{supp}}^{\mathrm{WKB}}$ (dotted orange line). This reduces suppressed SLF power fraction somewhat, but not enough to restore internally driven IGWs as a viable origin for magnetic SLF variability, as a substantial SLF power below $
u_{\mathrm{supp}}^{\mathrm{WKB}}$ are still observed.
Summary of results and observations for HD 108.

title: Faint and Fast Transients from Double Detonations of Low Mass White Dwarfs
authors: Miranda Pikus, Abigail Polin, Dillon Hasenour, Paul Duffell
abstract: There is significant evidence that white dwarfs can explode via the double detonation mechanism, whereby an initial detonation in an accreted helium shell triggers a second detonation of the carbon-oxygen core. This scenario has been invoked for white dwarfs near a solar mass to produce Type Ia-like supernovae, but low-mass explosions have been relatively unexplored despite the most common white dwarf being near 0.6 solar masses. We predict faint and fast transients emerging from double detonations of white dwarfs with total masses around 0.6 solar masses and accreted helium shells up to 0.3 solar masses. The models are computed through the moving-mesh nuclear hydrodynamics code Cattails and the Monte Carlo radiation transport code Sedona. A continuum of core-powered and shell-powered transients are produced with no more than 0.03 solar masses of radioactive nickel in the core or shell material, respectively. The light curves are rapid and sub-luminous, peaking near -17 magnitudes within 5 to 10 days. The ejecta is dominated by intermediate mass elements and unburnt core that imprint noticeable features in the spectrum. This is the first parameter survey to investigate double detonations at such low masses, and these systems could produce a historically missed population of supernovae. Our predictive models could help large sky surveys find these events.
comments: 14 pages, 4 figures, submitted to ApJ

figs.cap: Example density (dotted line) and temperature (solid line) profiles for an initial progenitor star model with $M_{\text{tot}}=$0.6\text{\,}\mathrm{M}_{\odot} and $M_{\text{shell}}=$0.2\text{\,}\mathrm{M}_{\odot}.

The top row are ejecta compositions for $M_{\text{tot}}=$0.6\text{\,}\mathrm{M}_{\odot} with varying shell masses. The vertical axis is mass fraction for a species. The bottom horizontal axis is enclosed mass in $M_{\odot}$ while the top horizontal axis is velocity in $\text{\,}\mathrm{k}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{/}\mathrm{s}$. The legend denotes which isotope group belongs to which color and the grey highlighted region denotes the shell material to guide the eye. The bottom row represents total yields of unburnt carbon and radioactive chromium, iron, and nickel as a function of shell mass. The compositions as a function of shell mass describe the distinct scenarios of radioactive material present in the ejecta, creating a continuum ranging from a primarily core-powered to a shell-powered transient.

Light curves and spectra for $M_{\text{tot}}=$0.6\text{\,}\mathrm{M}_{\odot}. The left column displays absolute AB magnitude in $ugriz$ filters for each model labeled by $M_{\text{core}}+M_{\text{shell}}$. The bottom axis is days since explosion while the top axis is days since $r$-peak. Our models assume LTE, so a shaded grey region in the light curves denote when NLTE effects begin to dominate (i.e. daughter decay tails). The right column shows spectra for each model at three different times since $r$-peak. Different spectral features are highlighted in colored vertical lines with colors grouping the same species. The rest wavelengths are blue shifted by a characteristic bulk velocity to guide the eye to prominent feature minima, where the bulk velocity is an abundance-weighted velocity for each model and each isotope.

Comparisons of our models with known observations (left panel: photometry, right panel: spectra). The colored lines are our double detonation models. The grey markers are photometric observation and the black lines are a selected spectrum observation. Our models are named based on their total and shell mass (for example, ‘0602’ means $M_{\text{tot}}=$0.6\text{\,}\mathrm{M}_{\odot} with $M_{\text{shell}}=$0.2\text{\,}\mathrm{M}_{\odot}). The spectra are labeled by the day since $r$-peak. The grey shaded portion of the light curve panel denotes the approximate time that the ejecta has become optically thin and the LTE assumption breaks down (i.e. daughter decay tails).

title: "Helium Enrichment Law": The Relation Between Helium and Metal Enrichment in Stars in FIRE-3 Simulations of Milky Way-mass Galaxies
authors: Pratik J. Gandhi, Earl P. Bellinger, Andrew Wetzel, Jeremy Bailin, Sarbani Basu, Isabella L. Trierweiler, Francisco J. Mercado
abstract: Helium abundance is a key input to stellar models that are used to infer accurate ages, masses, and compositions for individually resolved stars in the Milky Way (MW), underpinning Galactic archaeology. Since spectroscopically measuring He abundances is difficult, stellar models often assume a fixed "chemical enrichment law" dY/dZ (the slope linearly relating a star's helium mass fraction Y to its metal mass fraction Z). If incorrect, this assumption can introduce significant systematics in inferring stellar properties. Using the FIRE-3 cosmological baryonic zoom-in simulations, we investigate helium versus metal enrichment in the stars of MW-mass galaxies. Given the nucleosynthetic yields in FIRE-3, overall metal production is dominated by core-collapse supernovae (CCSN) at all progenitor metallicities. He production is dominated by CCSN for progenitor metallicities of Z <= 0.1 Zsun, but by stellar winds for progenitors near Zsun. Our simulations produce a range of dY/dZ slopes slopes with best-fit values of ~0.75-2.1 depending on the age of the stars considered at present day; on average consistent with the range of values from MW observations but with no single "universal" enrichment law. The dY/dZ slope also shows galaxy-to-galaxy variance in our simulations, and to leading order increases over cosmic time within the same galaxy, based on the peculiarities of the formation histories of each MW-mass system. Despite choosing a fixed set of nucleosynthetic yields for stellar feedback processes in FIRE-3, we predict variance in dY/dZ for stars in MW-mass galaxies, and observations of MW stars must be interpreted in this context.
comments: 17 pages, 9 figures. Submitted to ApJ

figs.cap: Relative contributions of the three mechanical feedback channels in FIRE-3 to the helium and metal yields, as a function of time after star particle formation. We show the yields from stellar winds, core-collapse supernovae, and white dwarf supernovae per unit $\rm{M}_{\odot}$ formed, as a function of age of the simple stellar population (SSP). Left panel shows results for an SSP at $0.1\rm{Z_{\odot}}$, middle for $1\rm{Z_{\odot}}$, and right for $5\rm{Z_{\odot}}$, to demonstrate how the relative contributions of the feedback channels evolve as a function of progenitor SSP metallicity. The top row shows how total heavy metal yields (for elements C through Fe) are dominated by core-collapse supernovae at all progenitor metallicities, and mostly saturate by $\approx 250$ Myr after the birth of the SSP. The bottom row shows that core-collapse supernovae dominated helium yields at $\lesssim 0.1\,\rm{Z_{\odot}}$ and saturate within $\approx 400$ Myr, stellar wind helium yields become dominant at $\gtrsim 1\,\rm{Z_{\odot}}$, with an early-time contribution from O/B winds and a similar late-time (after $1$ Gyr) contribution from AGB winds.

Distribution of stellar $Z_{\rm initial}$ and $Y_{\rm initial}$ in our simulated galaxies at present day. Left panel shows the PDF of initial $Z$ for all stars within a $15$ kpc sphere centered on each galaxy, and we ignore any stars with $Z_{\rm initial}>0.05$ as shown by the grey shaded region (only $\sim 0.5\%$ of all stars). The PDFs for all three galaxies are consistent with each other to leading order, with similar median ($Z\approx 0.006-0.011$, or, $\approx 0.4-0.8\,\rm{Z_{\odot}}$) values as described in Section III.1. On the right, we show the PDF of $Y_{\rm initial}$ values for all stars within $15$ kpc spheres with $Z_{\rm initial}\leq 0.05$, as identified in the left panel. Again, we find consistent distributions across the three simulated MW-mass galaxies, with similar median ($Y\approx 0.248-0.255$, or, $\approx 0.92-0.95\,\rm{Y_{\odot}}$) values. The vertical dashed lines show max($Y_{\rm initial}$): $0.365$ for m12i, $0.378$ for m12q, and $0.369$ for m12b.

Stellar $Y_{\rm initial}$ versus $Z_{\rm initial}$ for our three simulated MW-mass galaxies. Top row: We plot abundances for all stars within a $15$ kpc sphere from the galactic center in each simulation, and exclude the minimal population ($<5\%$) of star particles with $Z>0.05$. Bottom row: Only stars in the Solar annulus in each simulation, with $Z\leq 0.05$. We color-code the plots by the average age at $z=0$ of the star particles in each hex bin. The dashed grey lines in each panel show different $\Delta Y$/$\Delta Z$ slopes to guide the eye, and the range from $0.0$ to $3.0$ brackets the full range suggested by fits to observed MW stars. The primary takeaway from each of the three simulations is that at $z=0$, stars lie along a wide range of $\Delta Y$/$\Delta Z$ slopes and do not conform to a specific, narrow range in slopes. However, the Solar annulus sample shows a smaller spread in $Y-Z$ space, and does not contain stars with highly super-Solar abundances (most of which lie in the bulge and inner galaxy in our simulations). Each simulation however, predicts a somewhat different variation of the slope with stellar age. Finally, we see that the youngest stars in each simulation ($\sim 0-2$ Gyr at present day) inhabit a narrower range in the Y-Z plane than older stars, although its precise slope varies across the three galaxies.

Variation in the helium enrichment relation over cosmic time. For each galaxy (m12i in magenta, m12q in blue, m12b in gold) the curves show the best-fit $\Delta Y$/$\Delta Z$ value in bins of stellar age, and shaded regions show $1\sigma$ scatter. Scatter points show values computed using stars of all ages, corresponding to the values listed in Table 2. Top: for all stars within $15$ kpc from the galaxies’ centers. Bottom: for only Solar annulus stars. Both panels demonstrate that to leading order $\Delta Y$/$\Delta Z$ increased as the galaxies built up over cosmic time, although galaxy-to-galaxy variations are present in individual stellar age bins depending on the specifics of each system’s SFH. Broadly, $\Delta Y$/$\Delta Z$ ranges from $\approx 0.5-1.0$ for the oldest stars to $\approx 1.25-2.50$ for those younger than roughly $6$ Gyr. In each galaxy, the Solar annulus sample shows shallower slopes than the “all stars” sample, by $\approx 0.25-0.50$; again, the specific value depends on the galaxy’s formation history.

Star formation histories of our three simulated galaxies. Left: the star formation rate (SFR) for each galaxy in $\rm{M_{\odot}}\,\rm{yr}^{-1}$ as a function of lookback time (with $\approx 13.7$ Gyr ago being the Big Bang and $0$ Gyr being present day). m12i is in magenta, m12q in blue, and m12b in gold. We average the SFR over a running baseline of $0.01$ Gyr, or $10$ Myr, to highlight the inherently “bursty” (stochastic) nature of star formation. Broadly, we show that the three galaxies have similar SFHs barring burstiness, with a few key differences: m12q and m12b show higher SFRs than m12i at lookback times $\gtrsim 11$ Gyr ago, m12b has the lowest SFR at $4\lesssim t_{\rm lookback}\lesssim 8$ Gyr, m12i shows a dip in SFR for $3.5\lesssim t_{\rm lookback}\lesssim 6$ Gyr, and most importantly m12b shows dramatic dips in SFR at lookback times of $\approx 2$ and $\approx 1$ Gyr, while m12i and m12q show relatively steady, slightly increasing, star formation from $\approx 2$ Gyr to present day. Right: the cumulative stellar mass growth histories of the galaxies relative to their final mass versus lookback time. The variations in SFR on the left map onto differences on the right.

Stellar enrichment histories of our three simulated galaxies. Left: the overall enrichment in the heavy metal mass fraction of stars $Z$, versus lookback time from the Big Bang ($\approx 13.7$ Gyr) to present day ($0$ Gyr). Right: enrichment in the helium mass fraction of stars $Y$ versus lookback time from the Big Bang to present day. The solid lines show the median value across all stars in the galaxy at the specific times, and the shaded regions show the $68\%$ scatter, with m12i in magenta, m12q in blue, and m12b in gold. In both panels, we compute median and $68\%$ values over a running $100$ Myr baseline. Overall, the three galaxies show increasing enrichment in stars and the ISM (since the composition of stars formed at a given time reflects the composition of the gas they formed out of) in both heavy metals and helium over time; however, there is significant variance in how quickly each galaxy enriches at given cosmic time (corresponding to the details of their star formation rates at that time). Also, we highlight the drops in metal/helium mass fraction that occur in each galaxy, with the most significant ones occurring at lookback times of $\approx 3$ Gyr (m12i), $\approx 4$ Gyr (m12q), and $\approx 2$ Gyr (m12b) — these are the result of a significant merger with a more metal-poor lower-mass galaxy or a significant inflow of more pristine gas from the cosmic web, resulting in an influx of hydrogen and therefore lower $Z$ and $Y$. For an alternative view, see Appendix A and Figure 9.

title: JWST/MIRI Observations of Amorphous Silicates in Interstellar Comet 3I/ATLAS
authors: Cristina A. Thomas, Michael S. P. Kelley, David E. Harker, Martin A. Cordiner, Davide Farnocchia, Dennis Bodewits, Steven B. Charnley, Maria N. Drozdovskaya, Marco Micheli, Stefanie N. Milam, Cyrielle Opitom, Silvia Protopapa, Nathan X. Roth, Megan E. Schwamb
abstract: We present JWST/MIRI Low Resolution Spectroscopy (LRS) of 3I/ATLAS obtained post-perihelion at a heliocentric distance of 2.21 au. Our spectrum contains a prominent 10 micron silicate emission feature with a broad, smooth shape that is distinct from those commonly observed in Solar System comets. We model the spectrum using thermal emission from amorphous carbon, amorphous olivine, and amorphous pyroxene grains. Our models strongly favor a pyroxene-dominated, amorphous silicate composition and show a degeneracy between silicate grain size and the relative abundance of silicate and carbon dust. Across a set of representative models, the best-fitting crystalline abundance is zero, and we place an upper limit of 5.3% on the crystalline fraction of the silicates. We identify an emission feature near 6.83 microns that is consistent with aliphatic C-H-bearing material. The overwhelmingly amorphous silicate composition supports previous work that measured unusual volatile and isotopic composition in suggesting that the material incorporated into the object experienced little thermal processing and preserves information about the conditions in which this interstellar planetesimal formed.
comments: submitted to ApJL

figs.cap: Left: Extracted 3I spectral flux using the LRS pipeline point and extended settings compared to our coma-corrected point source method. Right: A comparison of the normalized emissivity spectrum using the extended source pipeline products and our coma-corrected point source method. The extended source extraction shows a fundamentally different shape for the 10 $\mu$m emissivity feature including significant artifacts around 10-12 $\mu$m. As a result, the spectrum from the extended-source extraction cannot reliably characterize the dust mineralogy.

Comparison of 10 $\mu$m silicate emission feature shapes, adapted from [32] to include 3I/ATLAS. The relative emissivity spectra are continuum subtracted and normalized to 1.0 at 9.3 $\mu$m. The distinct shape of the 3I silicate feature demonstrates its unusual mineralogy relative to Solar System comets. 17P/Holmes, 46P/Wirtanen, and 73P-C/Schwassmann–Wachmann 3 are highlighted and all other comet spectra with well-defined silicate bands are shown as thin gray lines. A vertical line at 8.25 µm marks the location of a feature in the 17P and 73P spectra, a line at 9.3 µm marks the normalization point, lines at 9.95 and 11.15 µm mark the locations of Mg-rich crystalline olivine features in the spectra of 17P and 73P.

Joint posterior distribution for $\log_{10}(\mathrm{sil}/\mathrm{car})$ versus $a_{p,\mathrm{sil}}$. $\Delta\ln P$ denotes the calculated difference from the maximum profile likelihood. The colors show solutions within $\Delta\ln P>$ -10, -5, and -2 of the best-fitting model. The relationship between silicate abundance and silicate peak grain size is clear across a space of high-probability solutions.

Left: The calculated ridge of solutions through the $\log_{10}(\mathrm{sil}/\mathrm{car})$ versus $a_{p,\mathrm{sil}}$ parameter space. Solutions A-E correspond to the 10th, 30th, 50th, 70th, and 90th percentiles in $a_{p,\rm sil}$ among solutions with $\Delta\ln P>-5$. Right: 3I/ATLAS emissivity spectrum compared to the modeled spectra for solutions A-E. All solutions are reasonable fits to the silicate emissivity feature. Our dust model does not include the emission feature observed at 6.83 $\mu$m.

title: Little Red Dots with Broad H$β$ Lines Reveal the Black Hole Mass Function at 7<z<9.5
authors: Anthony J. Taylor, Steven L. Finkelstein, Hollis B. Akins, Vasily Kokorev, Pablo Arrabal Haro, Sophie Koudmani, Caitlin M. Casey, Mark Dickinson, Junehyoung Jeon, Madisyn Brooks, Volker Bromm, Christopher J. Conselice, Kelcey Davis, Callum T. Donnan, Andreas L. Faisst, Seiji Fujimoto, Lukas J. Furtak, Mauro Giavalisco, Ansh R. Gupta, Michaela Hirschmann, Tiger Yu-Yang Hsiao, Dale D. Kocevski, Anton M. Koekemoer, Gene C. K. Leung, Ray A. Lucas, Lorenzo Napolitano, Casey Papovich, Laura Pentericci, Pablo G. Perez-Gonzalez, Rachel S. Somerville, Fabian Walter, L. Y. Aaron Yung
abstract: We present a systematic search for broad H$\beta$ emission at $7<z<9.5$ in 21,770 JWST/NIRSpec PRISM spectra drawn from four blank fields and six lensing clusters with photometry spanning 1942 arcmin$^2$. We find a sample of 20 sources with statistically significant broad-H$\beta$ emission, including 13 new sources. Our entire sample has colors and morphologies consistent with little red dots (LRDs), compared to only 37\% of broad-line emitters at $3.5<z<6$. Interpreting the broad-lines as indicators of Broad-line Active Galactic Nuclei (BLAGN), we infer black hole masses of $4.2\times10^{6}-2.1\times10^{8}$\,$M_{\odot}$. We calculate completeness corrections and construct the black hole mass function at $z\sim8$. The normalization of the black hole mass function rises by $\approx1.0$~dex from $z\sim8-5$, consistent with average black hole growth at $f_{\textrm{Edd}}\approx0.1$. Comparing with cosmological simulations, the $z\sim8$ black hole mass function requires heavy ($10^5$\,$M_{\odot}$) seeds or super-Eddington accretion onto light or intermediate mass seeds to match its normalization. Finally, we infer bolometric luminosities for the sample and construct a bolometric luminosity function. We integrate over this luminosity function to derive a black hole accretion density (BHAD) of $4.8^{+5.8}_{-2.6}\times10^{-7}~M_{\odot}~\textrm{yr}^{-1}~\textrm{Mpc}^{-3}$, showing broad agreement with previous photometric work, but disagreement with previous X-ray models, reinforcing the idea that BLAGN are more common in the early universe than previously expected.
comments: 24 pages, 9 figures, 6 tables. Submitted to ApJ

figs.cap: Upper Panel: Completeness (colored shading) for a five hour PRISM exposure as a function of broad-H$\beta$ flux and broad-H$\beta$ FWHM at $z=8.5$. Solid overplotted lines are contours of logarithmic black hole mass (in solar masses) [64, as computed with], and dashed overplotted lines are contours of Eddington ratio (assuming unattenuated Case B recombination [H$\alpha$/H$\beta=2.86$] and a 130$\times$ bolometric correction from H$\alpha$ flux to bolometric luminosity). Our sample is highly detection complete above $10^{7.5}$ $M_{\odot}$, and is consistent with Eddington ratios $\leq 1$. Lower panel: Contours of exposure time corresponding to 50% completeness in broad-H$\beta$ flux and broad-H$\beta$ FWHM space at $z=8.5$. Here, both contours and colored points (the BLAGN sample) are colored by exposure time. Points that are a darker shade than their overlapping contours are objects with significantly lower completeness, while objects with lighter shades than overlapping contours are highly complete. As expected, increased exposure times offer sensitivity to fainter line fluxes, and have little to no effect on FWHM sensitivity.

JWST-based black hole mass functions at $z\sim 5$ [134, 111, 51, hollow points;] and $z\sim 8$ (solid points). For this work, we show both the completeness corrected points as solid red circles, and the equivalent black hole mass function without a completeness correction as grey squares. The black hole mass function shows significant ($>3.5\sigma$) evolution over $z\sim 5-8$ in all but the two heaviest mass bins where number statistics limit the significance to $2.0\sigma$ and $1.4\sigma$ respectively.

Left panel: The $L_{\textrm{bol}}$ luminosity function for the full $z\sim 8$ H$\beta$-emitter sample computed using the [66] $L_{\textrm{bol}}/L_{5100}$ correction, as well as recent literature results from LRDs. This luminosity function falls off rapidly at $L_{\textrm{bol}}\sim 10^{45}$ erg s$^{-1}$ and appears to extend in a power-law-like manner to lower luminosities (omitting the lowest luminosity highly incomplete data point). The red curve and shaded region shows the median and 68% confidence interval Schechter function fit to the most luminous three data points from this work. Right panel: The BHAD as a function of redshift. We also overplot the cosmic star-formation rate density from [67] re-normalized by a factor of 3000 to match the BHAD at $z\sim 3$ as a point of reference. Our detected BLAGN sample produces a result that broadly agrees with a photometric LRD sample from [140]. This sample was initially introduced in [3] using non-LRD specific assumptions and was reprocessed with LRD-specific corrections by [140]. We find good agreement with the BHAD derived from the $M_{H,L}=10^{8}M_{\odot}$ models of [79], a simulation in which BHs are seeded and grow within atomic cooling halos. We note that our data are likely a lower limit on the true BHAD, as they do not account for obscured, non-broad-line AGN.

The UV luminosity functions of the $z\sim 8$ BLAGN sample in this work and the $z\sim 5$ BLAGN sample from [134] compared to pre-JWST luminosity functions from [53]. We plot the best fit galaxy+AGN UV luminosity function at $z=8$ from [53] as a solid dark blue curve, and we shade the region between their AGN best-fit curve where the AGN UV luminosity function was permitted to turn over (dashed dark blue curve) and their AGN best-fit curve where the AGN UV luminosity function was fit as a power-law to faint magnitudes (dotted dark blue curve). We plot the early-JWST galaxy+AGN UV luminosity function from [19] at $z=8.7$ as the dashed green curve. At both $z\sim 5$ and $z\sim 8$, BLAGN are $\sim 1-2$ dex more abundant at all UV luminosities than pre-JWST fits predicted, and the $z\sim 8$ objects appear to make up $\sim 2-10\%$ of the objects at the bright end of the luminosity function.

Left: The reprocessed black hole mass functions from [134] and this work separated into LRDs and non-LRDs. Downward pointing triangles indicate $1\sigma$ upper limits in mass bins occupied by fewer than one object (see §V.1). The non-LRDs are not present at $z\sim 8$, and thus show significant evolution, while the LRDs show only moderate evolution. Right: Here, we decrease all of the LRD masses by a factor of 10 in an approximation of the results of [127]. At $z\sim 5$, this modification causes the black hole mass function to be completely dominated by non-LRDs at all masses.

This work’s observed black hole mass functions compared to literature models from [136], [81], and [98] at $z\sim 5$ (left panel) and $z\sim 8$ (right panel). Here we plot the models using $10^{2}$ $M_{\odot}$, $10^{3}$ $M_{\odot}$, and $10^{5}$ $M_{\odot}$ seeds from [98], models from [81] at $5<z<6$ and $7<z<10$ that use heavy seeds limited to Eddington accretion rates and light seeds permitted to accrete at super-Eddington rates, and models from [136] that use heavy seeds with both an Eddington limited model, and a super-Eddington-permitted model. Eddington limited light seeds curves for all three simulations do not produce black holes with $M_{\textrm{BH}}>10^{6}\,M_{\odot}$, and are thus excluded from these figures. This suggests that heavy seeding (solid curves) and/or highly super-Eddington accretion is necessary and prevalent at high redshifts to match observations, regardless of the treatment of LRD mass.

title: Effects of Dust in Electron-Capture Supernovae: Difficulty in Explaining Intermediate Luminosity Red Transients
authors: Yuma Takeichi, Daichi Tsuna, Daichi Hiramatsu, Morgan MacLeod, Masato Sato
abstract: The progenitors of intermediate-luminosity red transients (ILRTs) spanning the luminosity gap between novae and supernovae are under debate, and electron-capture supernovae (ECSNe) have been proposed as a strong candidate. ECSNe from super asymptotic giant branch (super-AGB) stars have been theoretically predicted to be much brighter than ILRTs, but attenuation by dusty winds of their super-AGB progenitors may ease this tension. Here we construct a semi-analytical framework for calculating the light curves of ECSNe with dust attenuation and re-emission, by combining recent ECSN light curve predictions with a model for dust physics. Even by varying both the wind mass-loss rate and the ECSN model parameters, we find it challenging to simultaneously fit the light curve and color evolution of ILRTs. This poses a potential challenge to the standard models of ECSNe for explaining ILRTs. For explaining ILRTs, we propose either the existence of a population of ECSNe with much lower explosion energies ($\sim$10$^{48}$-$10^{49}$ erg) and dimmer plateaus, or alternative model(s) to ECSNe that realize such low explosion energies.
comments: 20 pages, 12 figures

title: The UKIRT M33 Monitoring Project - VII. A 15-year K-band photometric catalogue of long-period variable stars in the central kiloparsec of M33
authors: Mina Alizadeh, Atefeh Javadi, Yousefali Abedini, Fatemeh Nikzat, Hedieh Abdollahi, Jacco Th. van Loon
abstract: We present a homogenised K-band photometric catalogue for the central ${\approx}12$ arcmin$^2$ (${\approx}0.9$ kpc$^2$) of the Triangulum spiral galaxy M33, combining four independent PSF-based near-infrared datasets obtained with UKIRT between 2003 and 2018. These comprise the 2003-2007 UIST multi-epoch monitoring survey, the 2005 UFTI K-band mosaic (for which we present new PSF photometry), new WFCAM PSF reductions for the four central tiles, and a single K-band epoch from the 2018 UKIRT Hemisphere Survey (UHS DR3). Cross-matching all four catalogues and retaining stars detected in at least two of them yields 847 unique stars comprising 21,085 valid K-band measurements spanning a baseline of 15.11 yr. Photometric homogenisation onto the 2MASS/Vega system via 82 low-scatter calibration stars removes systematic inter-dataset offsets of up to 0.22 mag. Of the 847 monitored stars, 771 (91 per cent) are classified as variable ($\sigma_{\rm rms} > 0.10$ mag), including 385 high-amplitude variables ($A_K \geq 1.0$ mag): prime Mira-type long-period variable candidates for period determination. Cross-matching with archival Spitzer IRAC photometry yields 156 matched stars, of which 120 satisfy $\langle K\rangle - [3.6] > 0.5$ mag, identifying dust-enshrouded AGB candidates inaccessible to all-sky optical surveys. This catalogue constitutes the most extensive near-infrared photometric baseline assembled for AGB stars in any spiral galaxy beyond the Milky Way, providing the photometric foundation for the period-luminosity analysis and star-formation-history reconstruction in the companion Paper VIII. The full catalogue is available at the Centre de Données astronomiques de Strasbourg (CDS).
comments: Accepted for publication in MNRAS

title: A Fast and Memory-Efficient Algorithm for Searching Faint Moving Objects using Synthetic Tracking
authors: Chengxing Zhai, Albert J. Zhai
abstract: Detecting unknown faint moving objects using optical imaging is challenging. Long exposure times are infeasible for such targets, as the resulting image streaking causes a loss of signal-to-noise ratio due to energy dispersal across multiple pixels. To address this, synthetic tracking, a track-before-detect method, replaces long exposures with many short exposures, integrating them in post-processing to recover the moving signal. Enabled by modern CMOS detectors with fast readout and low read noise, this technique synthesizes telescope tracking by searching over a grid of velocities. However, the conventional brute-force implementation imposes a significant computational burden: integrating N_f frames of size (N_x,N_y) requires O(N_x N_y N_f^3) operations. This cost becomes prohibitive for megapixel-scale frames with N_f~100. Although dynamic programming can reduce the computational complexity by a factor of N_f, it requires a prohibitive memory of O(N_x N_y N_f^2), unsuitable for large-format detectors. This article presents a novel algorithm to achieve the computational efficiency of dynamic programming while maintaining a memory footprint of just O(N_x N_y N_f) by slightly approximating the computation of frame shifts for alignment. By expressing the shift as a sum of terms proportional to the digits frame index in binary and rounding up each of these terms, frames can be integrated efficiently by hierarchically adding intermediate sums that are shared across different velocities with the same higher bits in binary. The approximation only introduces a small tracking error that increases logarithmically with the number of frames. This advancement enables synthetic tracking to be executed with high energy efficiency, making it practical for deployment on standard workstations rather than requiring high-performance computing infrastructure such as GPU servers or CPU clusters.
comments: 16 pages, 6 figures

title: A self-supervised machine learning approach to identify instrumental systematics in 21cm Cosmology
authors: Ajith Sampath
abstract: The primordial sound waves in the baryon-photon plasma are imprinted on the large-scale galaxy distribution as Baryon Acoustic Oscillations (BAO), serving as a cosmological standard ruler to constrain dark energy and the Hubble parameter. The upcoming 21cm intensity-mapping arrays are designed to map the 21cm emission across large volumes and measure the BAO scale. However, radio interferometers suffer from instrumental systematics that can hinder detection of the cosmological 21cm signal by leaking bright foregrounds into the signal-dominated modes. This work aims to demonstrate that a self-supervised model can predict the instrument systematic state (here, the amplitude of a spectral ripple in the beam width) in interferometric visibilities and potentially disentangle the instrument from the sky without a forward model. Based on the fact that an instrument stays the same as the sky rotates in a drift-scan observation, and that the same sky is observed under different instrument states, we train a convolutional autoencoder to compress the information in the simulated visibilities and separate this information into instrument-only and sky-only latent vectors. The result shows excellent prediction of the unknown instrument systematic for 15 held-out instrument states with $R^2 = 0.9975$ with a linear probe, against $R^2 = -3.55$ for a random-encoder baseline. The instrument-latent carries no detectable sky signal, as measured with a total-power sky proxy, for any held-out test data. The sky-latent vector and instrument-latent vector show partial separation but not complete disentanglement, identifying sky-latent purity as the primary open problem. The results show the ability of the model to recognize the systematic and show a promising path towards an ML-based foreground cleaning pipeline. Full instrument-sky disentanglement constitutes the natural next step.
comments: 14 pages, 8 figures

title: Cosmological Constraints on Interacting Dark Matter with SPT-3G D1
authors: Cynthia Trendafilova, Fei Ge, Ali Rida Khalife, Christian L. Reichardt
abstract: Models of the dark sector in which the dark matter participates in nontrivial interactions can create detectable signatures in cosmological observables, providing non-terrestrial means of probing the nature of dark matter. In this work, we test dark matter-baryon scattering, dark matter-dark radiation interactions, and dark matter annihilation using measurements of the CMB and BAO. We leverage the latest SPT-3G D1 CMB measurements of the primary anisotropies, alongside the D1 MUSE lensing data, to set up-to-date bounds on these models. From the combination of Planck, ACT DR6, and SPT-3G D1 data, we constrain the velocity-independent dark matter-baryon scattering cross-section to $\sigma_\mathrm{DM-b} < 4.6\times10^{-26}~\mathrm{cm^2}$, the dark matter-dark radiation momentum transfer rate to $\Gamma_\mathrm{0,nadm}<5.2\times10^{-8}\,\text{Mpc}^{-1}$, and the effective dark matter annihilation parameter, quantifying the fractional thermally averaged cross-section, to $p_\mathrm{ann}<3.7\times10^{-28}~\mathrm{cm^3/s/GeV}$, all at the 95% confidence level. The improved sensitivity to the first two models is in particular driven by the precision measurements of CMB lensing at small scales provided by SPT-3G D1 MUSE lensing data. For annihilating dark matter, due to the degeneracy of the effect with the optical depth to reionization, we observe a non-trivial relationship between the upper bound on $p_\mathrm{ann}$ and the large-scale polarization information. When combining CMB data with the latest measurements from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI), upper bounds on extended model parameters can appear to tighten as the model space attempts to accommodate the known discrepancy between these data. Future CMB and BAO measurements will provide better clarity on reconciling this discrepancy and enhance our ability to test dark matter interactions.
comments: 16 pages, 7 figures

figs.cap: The fractional change, relative to a $\Lambda$CDM cosmology, of the CMB lensed temperature ($TT$), polarization ($EE$), and lensing potential ($\phi\phi$) power spectra induced by non-zero dark matter-baryon scattering. The dark matter is assumed to scatter from all baryons, with $m_{\mathrm{DM}}=1$ GeV and an interaction fraction of 1. For each value of the velocity scaling $n_{\mathrm{b}}$, the cross-sections are chosen to be the same order-of-magnitude as the current upper bounds from CMB observations. The shaded areas show the bandpower measurement uncertainties from Planck, ACT DR6, and SPT-3G D1 centered around the $\Lambda$CDM predictions. In the primary CMB power spectra, the interaction creates a phase shift, since the tight coupling between dark matter and baryons changes the speed of sound in the primordial plasma. The scattering also induces a suppression of power at small scales, which is especially prominent for $n_{\mathrm{b}}\geq 0$ interactions, which were tightly coupled before recombination.

The fractional change, relative to a $\Lambda$CDM cosmology, of the CMB lensed temperature ($TT$), polarization ($EE$), and lensing potential ($\phi\phi$) power spectra due to dark matter interacting with dark radiation. The baseline $\Lambda$CDM case is shown in black lines; we also show a DMDR model (dashed green) and two of its variations, where either $\Gamma_{\mathrm{0,nadm}}$ (solid magenta) or $\Delta N_{\mathrm{eff}}$ (solid blue) is inflated by 10 fold. We also show a case where the additional light relics are all free-streaming species in the $\Delta N_{\mathrm{eff}}\times 10$ curve in dotted blue. Cosmological parameters used to produce these spectra are taken from the mean of an MCMC run with Planck data only. The shaded areas show the bandpower measurement uncertainties from Planck, ACT DR6, and SPT-3G D1 centered around the $\Lambda$CDM predictions.

The fractional change, relative to a $\Lambda$CDM cosmology, of the CMB lensed temperature ($TT$), polarization ($EE$), and lensing potential ($\phi\phi$) power spectra when including dark matter annihilation, in other words, nonzero $p_{\mathrm{ann}}$. We hold $\{\theta_{\mathrm{\Lambda CDM}}\}=\{A_{s},n_{s},\theta_{*},\omega_{c},\omega_{b},\tau_{\rm reio}\}$ fixed while computing the power spectra with $p_{\mathrm{ann}}=1.6\times 10^{-28}~\mathrm{cm^{3}/s/GeV}$ and $4\times 10^{-28}~\mathrm{cm^{3}/s/GeV}$. Note that $p_{\mathrm{ann}}=4\times 10^{-28}~\mathrm{cm^{3}/s/GeV}$ corresponds to the 95% C.L. upper limit from Section IV.3. The reference model is taken to be the CMB-SPA best-fit cosmology. The shaded areas show the bandpower measurement uncertainties from Planck, ACT DR6, and SPT-3G D1 centered around the $\Lambda$CDM predictions. The most significant effect of dark matter annihilation is a bump in the CMB $EE$ power spectrum at $10\lesssim\ell\lesssim 100$. The impact on CMB lensing due to dark matter annihilation is negligible.

Marginalized posteriors for $\sigma_{\mathrm{DM-b}}$ and $\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}$ for dark matter-baryon scattering with $n_{\mathrm{b}}=0$, from SPA without lensing (purple), SPA with lensing (green), and SPA + Lensing + DESI (orange). The constraint on $\Omega_{m}$ from DESI DR2 BAO is shown in the vertical gray bands. The cross-section is partially degenerate with the matter density in CMB lensing data. Consequently, adding DESI data, which prefers a lower value of $\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}$, shifts the posterior to lower values of $\sigma_{\mathrm{DM-b}}$ and decreases the upper limit.

Constraints on the parameters $\Omega_{m}$, $\Delta N_{\mathrm{eff}}$, and $\Gamma_{\mathrm{0,nadm}}$ in the DM-DR model from Planck + Lensing (red), SPT+ACT + Lensing (blue), SPA + Lensing (green), and SPA + Lensing + DESI (orange). Because the momentum transfer rate is partially degenerate with the matter density, the addition of DESI data pulls the posterior towards smaller values of $\Gamma_{\mathrm{0,nadm}}$. The grey shaded vertical bands corresponds to the DESI inferred value within $\Lambda$CDM at 1 and 2$\,\sigma$ [2].

The dashed-dotted lines show the constraints from SPA + Lensing (pink/black) and SPT + Lensing + DESI (yellow/black) in the absence of any $\tau_{\rm reio}$ prior or large-scale polarization likelihood. The grey horizontal band in the bottom panels represents the $\tau_{\mathrm{reio}}$ prior of $\tau_{\mathrm{reio}}\sim\mathcal{N}(0.051,0.006^{2})$. The constraints on $p_{\mathrm{ann}}$ are consistent and barely change with different data combinations when using the same $\tau_{\mathrm{reio}}\sim\mathcal{N}(0.051,0.006^{2})$ prior, but the upper bound on $p_{\mathrm{ann}}$ changes with different $\tau_{\mathrm{reio}}$ information.

title: The Role of Star Formation and Morphology in the Mass-Metallicity Relation of Galaxies at Cosmic Noon
authors: Farhanul Hasan, Marc Rafelski, Kalina V. Nedkova, Peter J. Watson, Debra M. Elmegreen, Bruce G. Elmegreen, Zahra Sattari, Vihang Mehta, Alaina Henry, Mitchell Revalski, Benedetta Vulcani, Grecco A. Oyarzun, Y.Sophia Dai, Xin Wang, Matthew A. Malkan, Claudia M. Scarlata, Matthew J. Hayes, Alexandra Le Reste, Andrew J. Battisti, Anahita Alavi, James Colbert, Hakim Atek, Michael Rutkowski, Tucker Jones, Ilias Goovaerts, Alexander Beckett, Andrew J. Bunker, Mason Huberty
abstract: We investigate the dependence of the mass-metallicity relation (MZR) on star formation and galaxy morphology at 1.7<z<3.5, using JWST/NIRISS wide-field slitless spectroscopy of >1000 galaxies. The observations span >85 arcmin^2 from the pure-parallel PASSAGE and OutThere surveys. We derive gas-phase metallicities using a Bayesian framework that combines multiple strong emission-line ratios calibrated against direct auroral-line metallicity measurements from JWST. We constrain stellar masses, star formation rates (SFRs), and morphological properties using ancillary HST and JWST imaging. We stack spectra by stellar mass to constrain the MZR over log(M*/M)~6.5-11, and find that it is well described by a second-order polynomial, with a steep low-mass slope and metallicities<10% solar at log(M*/M)<7.5. Additional stacking by SFR and morphology reveals strong evidence for a fundamental metallicity relation (FMR). Specifically, at log(M*/M)<9.5, galaxies with lower SFRs are more metal-rich than those with higher SFRs at fixed mass. At log(M*/M)<9.5, we find that larger galaxies, and those having lower SFR surface densities, bulges, and/or spiral features are significantly metal rich relative to their smaller, higher SFR surface density, bulge-less, and/or non-spiral counterparts. These results suggest the secondary dependencies of the MZR reflect variations in the baryon cycle, such that recent metal-poor gas accretion drives concentrated star formation and metallicity dilution, while structurally developed galaxies retain more chemically enriched gas reservoirs.
comments: Submitted to ApJ. Main text has 23 pages, including 10 figures. Comments welcome

title: A Quiet Night in the Millihertz Sky? LISA Forecasts from LIGO/Virgo/KAGRA Populations
authors: Ignacio Magaña Hernandez, Antonella Palmese
abstract: The high-mass black hole population inferred from ground-based observations can substantially affect the number of binaries detectable by the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA). We use population constraints based on data from the latest LIGO/Virgo/KAGRA Gravitational-Wave Transient Catalog (GWTC-5.0), as well as constraints from the O3 search for intermediate-mass black hole binaries, to forecast the number and masses of binary black holes detectable by LISA. Using the released GWTC-5.0 population posterior, we obtain $6.6^{+5.5}_{-2.2}$ expected detections with signal-to-noise ratio $>8$ in 4 years (median and $90\%$ credible interval). The alternative population models we consider use a broken power law with two or three Gaussian peaks for either the primary-mass distribution or a common mass distribution for both black holes. For the three-peak model with the common mass distribution, extrapolating from $300$ to $1000M_\odot$ roughly doubles the median expected number of LISA detections to $\sim14$. The upper end of its $90\%$ credible interval rises from tens to thousands of expected detections, although approximations may limit the reliability of the most extreme counts. For the reference GWTC-5.0 population, $39^{+22}_{-11}\%$ of the binaries detectable by LISA merge during the mission or within $10$ years after its end and are potential multiband sources. Essentially all of these mergers would be detectable by a reference Cosmic Explorer configuration if it is operating at merger. Ground-based measurements of the high-mass population can therefore inform both LISA forecasts and the prospects for observing the same binaries through inspiral and merger.

title: Galactic Dynamics Drives Cyclic Star Formation in Dipole Dwarf Galaxies
authors: Robel Geda, Akaxia Cruz, Alyson Brooks, Jenny E. Greene, Carrie Filion, Adrian M. Price-Whelan, Thomas R. Quinn, James Wadsley, Ben Keller
abstract: Dwarf galaxies are dark matter-dominated systems that are sensitive to feedback and display bursty star formation histories. This makes them ideal probes of the processes that regulate star formation. This work investigates the timescales of star formation rate (SFR) variability in isolated dwarf galaxies using high-resolution cosmological zoom-in simulations of $50$ dwarf galaxies drawn from the Marvelous Massive Dwarfs and Extended Marvelous Dwarfs simulation suites ($7.3 <$ \lmstar $< 9.1$). We measure star formation histories in $10$ Myr bins and characterize their variability with power spectral densities (PSDs). At the population level, the PSDs of both disk and non-disk galaxies follow a broken power-law, with a break timescale near $100$ Myr. Individually, our galaxies show both smooth and bursty star formation. A subset of disk galaxies show quasi-periodic SFR oscillations about their mean, which we refer to as cyclic star formation. The dominant timescale of these oscillations scales linearly with half-light radius and is approximated by the orbital period at that radius. Cyclic galaxies have Magellanic Spiral (Sm) morphologies and host lopsided dipole gas disks. In these systems, the bulk of the gas in the lopsided disk moves between its maximum and minimum distance from the galactic center, compressing the star-forming gas once per radial orbit and driving the SFR cycle. Cyclic star formation adds a narrow Lorentzian component to the PSD, peaked at radial orbital frequency of the disk ($\sim 200-500$ Myr), which is comparable to burst timescales inferred from observations.
comments: 27 pages, 12 figures

figs.cap: Welch power spectral density of $\log\,\mathrm{SFR}_{10}$ as a function of fluctuation timescale $\tau_{k}$ (bottom axis) and frequency $f_{k}$ (top axis) for disk (left) and non-disk (right) galaxies. Gray lines show the ${\rm PSD}_{\rm Welch}$ of individual galaxies. Solid lines show the mean of each subsample (for $\tau_{k}\leq 1$ Gyr) and shaded bands show the $1\sigma$ scatter. Red dashed lines show broken power-law fits to the mean ${\rm PSD}_{\rm Welch}$ and $1\sigma$ scatter, with the high-frequency slope $\beta_{\rm high}$, break timescale $\tau_{\rm b}$, and break amplitude $S_{\rm b}$ listed in each panel. SFHs are constructed in $\Delta t=10$ Myr bins from the formation time of all star particles residing in each galaxy at $z=0$. The two subsamples show broadly similar distributions, with a characteristic broken power-law that resembles a damped random walk ($\beta_{\rm low}=0,\ \beta_{\rm high}=2$).

Comparison of a cyclic (green, disk galaxy), bursty (black, non-disk galaxy), and smooth (orange, disk galaxy) SFH over the last $4$ Gyr prior to $z=0$ ($\Delta t=10\,\mathrm{Myr}$ bins). Left: $\log\,\mathrm{SFR}$ after subtracting a 1 Gyr boxcar moving mean. Right: FFT amplitude spectrum of the moving mean subtracted SFH as a function of fluctuation timescale. The cyclic galaxy exhibits a sharply peaked spectrum dominated by a single mode, indicating quasi-periodic SFR oscillations at a well-defined timescale. In the second row, though the bursty galaxy spans a wider mean subtracted SFR distribution, it lacks a dominating timescale that imprints structure into the SFH (stochastic and aperiodic variability). The smooth SFH in the bottom panels also shows stochastic and aperiodic variability, but lacks strong variability (low amplitudes across its frequency spectrum).

Each column shows both quantities as a function of total mass, stellar mass, $\log\,\mathrm{sSFR}_{10}$, and half-light radius. The size and masses are measured at $z=0$. The $\log\,\mathrm{sSFR}_{10}$ panels show the mean and $1$ standard deviation spread for the same mean-subtracted SFH over a window of $4$ Gyr. Both $\zeta_{\rm SFR}$ and $\tau_{\rm max}$ show a trend as a function of mass and $\log\,\mathrm{sSFR}_{10}$, particularly for the disk sample, though with some scatter. $\tau_{\rm max}$ shows a strong linear relation with size, especially for the disk-subsample.

The columns show projected density maps for dark matter, gas, stars, and young stars (age $<100$ Myr) within a $13$ kpc box at $z=0$. Each panel contains the total mass of each component within the halo (even if not visualized here). The young stars panel includes the total $\log{\rm SFR}_{100}$ of the galaxy at $z=0$ in the bottom left, which corresponds to the same age of the population visualized in that panel.

Gas dynamics of r568 over the last $1$ Gyr of the high snapshot cadence simulation. The top row shows a projected density map of the cold gas spanning one cyclic SFH oscillation. The top row also shows a contour of the stellar projected density ($\log\Sigma_{\star}=\{6,7,8\}$ $M_{\odot}\,$kpc$^{-2}$) in cyan and $R_{\rm e}$ at that snapshot (white dashed line). The second and third row of panels show cold gas particle mass histograms, for angular ($\theta$) and galactocentric radial ($R$) positions binned at each snapshot ($10$ Myr temporal bins). The galaxies are centered using their usual SSC and oriented face-on using the AM vector of the cold gas at $z=0$ as a fixed reference frame at all times. The mass histogram panels include a normalized version of the ${\rm SFR}_{10}$ at each snapshot for reference, with the SFR values shown in the right axis. The radial histogram shows $R_{\rm e}$ (white dashed line) and the cold gas COM (solid white line) at each timestep. The snapshots that correspond to the projected density maps (first row of panels) are shown as vertical dashed lines in the histograms. These panels show that the galaxy’s lopsidedness (which is apparent in $\theta$) carries the bulk of gas between apsis, creating density fluctuations relative to its mean, which results in cyclic fluctuations in SFR. Because the radial frequency is key for the star formation, the SFR shares the radial frequency of the gas, but with a $\sim\pi$ phase offset. Similarly, because of the lopsided mass distribution, the COM of the cold gas is offset from the galaxy center, showing the same frequency (phase shifted) as the SFR. Lastly, $R_{\rm e}$ remains relatively stable throughout the window.

title: What shapes the bright end of the UV luminosity function? Stellar mass, star-formation variability, and dust in JADES
authors: Amanda Stoffers, Sandro Tacchella, Benjamin D. Johnson, Brant Robertson, Roberto Maiolino, Andrew J. Bunker, Emma Curtis-Lake, A. Lola Danhaive, Qiao Duan, Francesco D'Eugenio
abstract: JWST surveys find more UV-bright galaxies at $z>10$ than galaxy-formation models predict, but the roles of recent star formation, stellar mass and dust remain uncertain. We analyse 1365 spectroscopically confirmed JADES galaxies at $3\leq z\leq9$, fitting NIRCam photometry and NIRSpec emission lines with \ceri. Our model includes flexible star-formation histories (SFHs) under three priors, two-component dust attenuation and nebular emission. We account for spectroscopic selection through population reweighting and assess the reliability of inferred trends. At $z=3$--5, rising SFHs are more common in low-mass galaxies, whereas most galaxies above $10^{9.5}\,{\rm M}_{\odot}$ have declining SFHs. The apparent increase in rising fractions with redshift cannot be distinguished from the adopted SFH prior alone. At fixed stellar mass, recent star formation is the strongest predictor of UV brightness. UV-brighter galaxies have higher recent SFRs, younger stellar populations and less attenuation at fixed SFR. Below $10^9\,{\rm M}_{\odot}$, they are also more likely to have rising SFHs, with odds increasing by up to a factor of 2.3 per magnitude brighter, although the strongest trend requires caution. In contrast, galaxies with $M_{\mathrm{UV}}<-20$ at $z=3$--5 are predominantly massive, and approximately half have declining SFHs. Dust partly offsets burst-driven UV brightening: attenuation increases with recent SFR and declines gradually after the inferred SFR peak. In model sensitivity tests, dust has the largest effect on bright-end counts, whereas removing galaxy-to-galaxy SFH scatter changes them by at most 0.17~dex. Thus, bursts can make low-mass galaxies unusually UV-bright for their mass, while the absolute bright end of the UVLF is primarily shaped by stellar mass and dust attenuation.

title: Measuring the magnetization profiles of galaxy groups and clusters
authors: Kritti Sharma, Vikram Ravi, Elisabeth Krause
abstract: Magnetic fields are vital in determining the physical conditions of baryons in massive halos. They are, however, notoriously difficult to observe. This impacts problems from our understanding of galaxy formation, to the observed deficit in the amplitude of thermal Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (tSZ) power spectrum that affects cosmological inferences. Although Faraday rotation measures (RMs) offer a direct probe of magnetic fields, it weights magnetic fields by the free-electron density. Several probes of free electrons, including fast radio burst (FRB) dispersion measures (DMs) and kinematic SZ (kSZ) effect, are now maturing into precision tools. We combine RM$^2$ stacks from SPICE-RACS around DESI galaxy groups and ROSAT clusters with optical depth profiles constrained jointly by the FRB DM-redshift relation and the kSZ effect, and obtain 95% upper limits on the rms line-of-sight magnetic field of $<3.9$-$11.6~\mu$G ($<2.3$-$6.4~\mu$G) in groups (clusters) for a 10~kpc coherence length. Combining these with thermal pressure profiles inferred from tSZ-shear cross-correlations, we obtain 95% lower limits on the plasma $\beta$ of $>0.31$ ($>11$) in groups (clusters). Although current constraints are only limits, we forecast a first detection with larger datasets from the Deep Synoptic Array (DSA). We present the first forecast of the DSA RM grid density ($\sim365$ RMs deg$^{-2}$), which when combined with 10$^4$ FRBs would measure the field in groups to $3$-$13\%$ precision, compared to current constraints of $38$-$75\%$. Although the interpretation of current measurements remains challenging owing to depolarization along turbulent halo sightlines and the unknown coherence length, larger samples and DSA/Square Kilometer Array observations may resolve these uncertainties by measuring polarization-fraction profiles and the RM structure function using extended radio sources, respectively.

title: The Spatially-Resolved Recent Star Formation History of the M81 Disk
authors: Vaishnav V. Rao, Eric F. Bell, Adam Smercina, Tobin M. Wainer, Andrew Dolphin, Benjamin Williams, Julianne J. Dalcanton
abstract: The nearby M81 galaxy---a tidally interacting $L^*$ spiral disk---offers a unique perspective on the interplay of secular and external processes in shaping galaxy properties. We present the most detailed, panoramic map of M81's stellar populations to date, using archival Hubble Space Telescope ACS photometry from the ANGST survey spanning the full optical extent of its disk. From color-magnitude diagram fitting, we recover spatially-resolved star formation histories (SFHs) over the last $\sim180\,$Myr. M81's global SFH is remarkably steady in the last $\sim180\,$Myr with slight enhancements seen $\lesssim15\,$Myr ago. The average SFR surface density rises toward the center before falling off within the innermost $\sim4\,$kpc. The disk is also notably lopsided, with the eastern half having formed $\sim50\%$ more stars than the western half over the same area---a trend missed by FUV-based SFR indicators due to dust systematics. Finally, the long-term SFHs of both M81 and M82 point to a pericenter passage $\sim1\,$Gyr ago. By identifying M81-M82 analogs in the TNG50 cosmological simulation, we rule out the more recent pericenter times of $150-220\,$Myr predicted by some works, as such passages are inconsistent with M81's undisturbed SFH over the last $\sim180\,$Myr. With this work, M81 becomes only the third $L^*$ spiral---after M31 and NGC 6946---to have its SFH spatially resolved across large areas of its disk.
comments: 24 pages, 13 figures, 2 tables; Accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal

title: Improving cosmological distance measurements at high redshift using Lyman-Alpha forest BAO reconstruction
authors: Boryana Hadzhiyska, Roger de Belsunce
abstract: The Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) measures baryon acoustic oscillations (BAO) in the Lyman-$\alpha$ (Lyman-alpha) forest and provides a robust probe of the expansion history in the matter-dominated era. Yet, non-linear structure formation broadens and shifts the BAO peak. To undo these effects, we extend standard Zel'dovich reconstruction, routinely applied to galaxy surveys, to the Lyman-alpha forest. We validate our methodology on large-volume idealized Lyman-alpha forest mocks painted on top of the \textsc{AbacusSummit} $N$-body simulations, using linear control variates to suppress sample variance and thereby reduce the error bars by a factor of up to $\approx \sqrt{50}$. In fully sampled periodic boxes, reconstruction halves the radial BAO damping scale and reduces the uncertainties on the radial ($\apar$) and transverse ($\aperp$) scaling parameters by $\approx25\%$ and $\approx15\%$, respectively. It also reduces the non-linear shift from $\Delta\apar=+0.3\%$ to $+0.10\pm0.07\%$, while $\aperp$ remains unbiased. To make this approach readily applicable to observational data, we demonstrate the impact of a survey mask with a DESI-like density of $50\,\mathrm{deg}^{-2}$. For this mask, we compare two approaches to estimate the displacement field: either directly from the Lyman-alpha forest or using an external tracer with a number density of $\bar n \simeq 10^{-3}\,h^3\mathrm{Mpc}^{-3}$, such as Lyman-break galaxies and Lyman-$\alpha$ emitters---both key targets for DESI-II. Both approaches give comparable gains and reduce the uncertainties on $\apar$ and $\aperp$ by $\approx 27\%$ and $\approx 10\%$, respectively, with mild improvements for futuristic high-density surveys with $160\,\mathrm{deg}^{-2}$. Correspondingly, the figure of merit improves by factors of $1.66$ for fully sampled boxes, $1.65$ for a DESI-like, and $1.76$ for a high-density survey.

figs.cap: Impact of BAO reconstruction in Fourier space: BAO feature of Model 1 before (gray) and after (blue) reconstruction in the wedge closest to the transverse direction (left) and in the radial wedge (right). The points are the mean over the 12 realizations (six phases and two lines of sight), divided by the smooth part of the best fit, with error bars from the scatter between the realizations. Over $0.15<k<0.35\,h{\text{Mpc}}^{-1}$, the rms of the best fit increases by $12\%$ in the transverse wedge and by $34\%$ in the radial wedge.

Impact of BAO reconstruction in configuration space: Same as Fig. 1 for the correlation function of Model 1 in four angular wedges, before (gray) and after (blue) reconstruction. The left column shows the raw simulations and the right column the linear control variates of Sec. 4.2. Dashed and dotted curves show the two lines of sight and solid lines their paired mean, with error bands from the scatter between the six phases. The shaded interval marks $85<r<115\,h^{-1}{\text{Mpc}}$.

BAO scaling parameters before and after reconstruction: Offsets $100(\alpha-1)$ of the radial (top) and transverse (bottom panel) BAO scaling parameters before (open) and after (filled) reconstruction, for the four forest models in Fourier space (left) and in configuration space (right of the vertical line), without (gray) and with (blue) linear control variates. Each point averages the two lines of sight within each phase; the error bars are standard errors over the six phases. We use the baseline model of Sec. 4.1 with the raw pre-reconstruction weights.

Precision gains for varying sightline densities: Precision gain, $G=\sigma_{\rm pre}/\sigma_{\rm post}$, for $\alpha_{\parallel}$ (top) and $\alpha_{\perp}$ (bottom) as a function of the sightline density, for self-reconstruction from the forest (Regime III, line) and for displacements from external halo samples with three number densities (Regime II, open symbols, slightly offset horizontally). Points are the central fits. The bars are not statistical errors: they span the three fit variants of Sec. 4.3, without the damping priors, with $k\leq 0.30\,h{\text{Mpc}}^{-1}$, and with the errors of each state rescaled by $\sqrt{\chi^{2}/{\rm dof}}$. The fully sampled forest, fitted in the same way, gives $1.38$ and $1.19$, matching Tab. 2.

BAO reconstruction for the cross-correlation: Same as Fig. 1 but for the cross-correlation of the Ly-$\alpha$ forest and a quasar catalog. Following baseline expectation, we find a marginal improvement in the transverse wedge with a noticeable improvement in the radial wedge.

Impact of smoothing radius on gain: Variation of the smoothing radius in the range $4\leq R\,[\,h{\text{Mpc}}^{-1}]\leq 20$ for Model 1, phase 000 and line-of-sight LOSz. The dotted horizontal line denotes the reference value pre-reconstruction and the dashed vertical line indicates our smoothing radius choice.
